guides.title: Scales, Keys and the Circle of Fifths
guides.summary: Where scales come from in the physics of vibrating strings, how the major and minor scales and their key signatures are built, what the circle of fifths actually shows, and how keys, chords, cadences and modulation fit together in practice.

sections.heading: What a Scale Is and Why Music Needs One
sections.body: A scale is a chosen set of pitches, arranged in order, out of which a piece of music is built. That sounds trivially simple, and the simplicity conceals the most important decision in the whole of music theory. The range of pitches available to a human ear is continuous: between the note we call C and the note we call D there are infinitely many frequencies, and a violin or a voice can produce any of them. Music does not use them. Almost every musical tradition on earth selects a small handful, typically between five and twelve, and treats every other frequency as out of tune. Understanding why that selection is made, and how the particular selection used in Western music arose, is what this subject is really about. The reason to select at all is memory and pattern. If every pitch were available and equally meaningful, no melody could be recognised, no two performers could play together, and no instrument could be built with fixed strings or holes. Restricting to a small set turns pitch into a language with a finite alphabet. Once the alphabet is fixed, the ear learns the relationships between its letters, and those learned relationships are what make a melody sound complete or unfinished, restful or straining. When a tune stops on the wrong note, everyone in the room feels it, including people who have never had a music lesson. That feeling is not mystical; it is the sound of a pattern learned from thousands of hours of listening being left unresolved. A key is the next layer up. A scale is a set of notes; a key is a scale plus a hierarchy, a sense that one note in the set is home. The note that feels like home is the tonic, and everything else in the key is heard in relation to it. The same seven notes, C D E F G A B, form the key of C major when C is treated as home and the key of A minor when A is, and the two sound profoundly different despite being played on identical piano keys. Key is therefore a matter of emphasis and context, not merely of ingredients. The circle of fifths, which is the third pillar of this subject, is the map that organises all the keys into a single closed loop, arranged so that neighbours on the circle are the keys most closely related to each other. It is simultaneously a mnemonic for key signatures, a diagram of harmonic distance, a guide to what chords belong together, a plan for how to move from one key to another, and a compact summary of the mathematical accident on which the entire Western tuning system rests. It is the most useful single diagram in music, and it repays understanding rather than memorising.

sections.heading: Pitch, Frequency and the Octave
sections.body: Pitch is the ear's interpretation of the frequency of a vibration. A guitar string vibrating 220 times per second produces the note A below middle C, written A3 and measured as 220 hertz. Double that frequency to 440 hertz and you get the A above, the tuning-fork A that orchestras tune to, called A4. Double it again to 880 and you get the next A up. That doubling relationship is the deepest fact in music, and it is remarkably universal. Notes an octave apart sound so alike that essentially every musical culture gives them the same name and treats them as versions of the same thing, a phenomenon called octave equivalence. Men and women singing the same tune an octave apart are heard as singing in unison, not in harmony. The reason appears to lie in the physics of how most musical sounds are made. A vibrating string, a column of air in a pipe, or a human vocal fold does not vibrate at one frequency alone; it vibrates simultaneously at a fundamental frequency and at whole-number multiples of it. A string sounding 220 hertz also produces components at 440, 660, 880, 1,100 hertz and so on, in a series called the harmonic series, and the relative strengths of those components are what make a violin sound different from a flute playing the same note. Because the second harmonic of a note is exactly the octave above it, the octave is already physically present inside every note the ear hears. Human hearing spans roughly 20 to 20,000 hertz in youth, about ten octaves, though sensitivity to pitch relationships is best between roughly 100 and 4,000 hertz, which is where nearly all melody lives. A piano covers 27.5 hertz at the bottom to 4,186 at the top, a little over seven octaves. Two conventions are worth fixing. The first is that pitch is perceived logarithmically: what the ear registers as an equal step is an equal ratio of frequencies, not an equal difference. Going from 100 to 200 hertz sounds like the same distance as going from 400 to 800, though one spans 100 hertz and the other 400. Every calculation in music theory therefore multiplies and divides frequencies rather than adding and subtracting them. The second is the cent, a unit invented in the nineteenth century by Alexander Ellis for exactly this purpose. One octave is defined as 1,200 cents, and one semitone in modern tuning is exactly 100. A difference of about 5 cents is roughly the smallest most listeners can detect between successive notes, though beating between simultaneous notes reveals differences much smaller than that. The reference point itself is a convention rather than a law of nature. A4 was fixed at 440 hertz by international agreement in 1939 and confirmed as ISO 16 in 1955, but Baroque ensembles commonly tune to 415, a semitone lower, and many modern orchestras drift to 442 or 443 for a brighter sound. Pitch standards in the eighteenth century varied from roughly 380 to 480 hertz between cities.

sections.heading: Where Intervals Come From: The Harmonic Series
sections.body: If a scale is a selection of pitches, the obvious question is why those pitches and not others. The oldest and best answer comes from the harmonic series, and it explains the structure of Western music with surprising economy. A vibrating string of a given length has a fundamental mode in which the whole string swings as one, and it simultaneously vibrates in halves, thirds, quarters and so on. Those subdivisions produce frequencies at exactly two, three, four, five times the fundamental. Take a low C at about 65 hertz as a fundamental. The second harmonic at 130 hertz is the C an octave up, a 2:1 ratio. The third, at 195 hertz, is the G above that, a 3:2 ratio above the second harmonic, which we call a perfect fifth. The fourth, 260 hertz, is another C. The fifth, 325 hertz, is an E, a 5:4 ratio above the fourth harmonic, which we call a major third. The sixth is G again. The seventh is a flattish B flat that does not match any note on a piano. The pattern is striking. The simplest possible frequency ratios, 2:1, 3:2, 4:3, 5:4, 6:5, correspond exactly to the intervals Western music treats as most consonant: the octave, perfect fifth, perfect fourth, major third and minor third. This is not a coincidence of taste. When two notes with simple ratios sound together, their harmonic series overlap extensively, so the combined sound contains few clashing near-coincidences. When two notes have complex ratios, their harmonics fall close to one another without matching, producing the rapid beating and roughness the ear reports as dissonance. The German physicist Hermann von Helmholtz set out this account in 1863 in his book On the Sensations of Tone, and while modern psychoacoustics has refined it, adding the role of learning, culture and critical bandwidth in the cochlea, the core insight has held up well. The series also explains why brass instruments behave as they do. A natural trumpet or a bugle has no valves and can sound only the harmonics of its tube, which is why bugle calls use just four or five notes and why they are the notes of a major triad. Valves and slides were added precisely to fill in the gaps that the harmonic series leaves. The same logic governs the harmonics a guitarist produces by touching a string lightly at its halfway or third point. Two honest caveats belong here. First, consonance is not purely physical; what a culture treats as acceptable varies enormously, and intervals considered harsh in one tradition are structural in another. Second, instruments whose overtones are not whole-number multiples, such as bells, gongs and many drums, produce quite different consonance relationships, which is precisely why gamelan tunings, built around metallophones with inharmonic spectra, sound coherent on their own instruments and out of tune on a piano. The harmonic series explains the Western system; it does not legislate for all music.

sections.heading: Stacking Fifths and the Twelve-Note Chromatic Scale
sections.body: The perfect fifth, the 3:2 ratio, is the strongest relationship after the octave itself, and it is the generator of the entire Western note system. The procedure, credited to the Pythagoreans in the sixth century BC and almost certainly older in practice, is to start on a note and repeatedly go up a fifth, folding each result back down into a single octave whenever it climbs out of range. Start on C. A fifth up gives G. A fifth above G gives D. Then A, E, B, F sharp, C sharp, G sharp, D sharp, A sharp, E sharp or F, and a fifth above that returns to something very close to C. Written as a chain: C, G, D, A, E, B, F sharp, C sharp, A flat, E flat, B flat, F, and back to C. Twelve steps, twelve distinct notes, and the chain closes on itself. Those twelve notes, arranged in ascending order within one octave, are the chromatic scale: C, C sharp, D, D sharp, E, F, F sharp, G, G sharp, A, A sharp, B. Each adjacent pair is a semitone apart, the smallest interval in standard Western music, and two semitones make a whole tone. The chain does not actually close exactly, and this is one of the most consequential facts in music history. Twelve perfect fifths multiply the frequency by three halves twelve times, which is 3 to the twelfth over 2 to the twelfth, or 531,441 divided by 4,096, about 129.746. Seven octaves multiply it by 2 to the seventh, which is 128. The two are not equal. The ratio between them, 531,441 to 524,288, or about 1.0136, is called the Pythagorean comma and amounts to roughly 23.46 cents, close to a quarter of a semitone. It is small but audible, and every tuning system in history is an attempt to deal with it. The chromatic scale is therefore not a natural object handed down by physics but a compromise: twelve happens to be the smallest number of equal divisions of the octave that produces a very good approximation to the pure fifth and a tolerable one to the pure third. In twelve-tone equal temperament the fifth is 700 cents against a pure 701.955, an error of under 2 cents that almost nobody can hear. Other divisions work too. Nineteen and thirty-one equal divisions give better major thirds and have been used experimentally, and fifty-three divisions approximates both fifth and third almost perfectly. Twelve won because it is small enough to be practical on keyboards and fretted instruments and good enough for the ear. Naming needs one convention. The same key on a piano can be called C sharp or D flat, depending on the musical context. These are enharmonic equivalents: identical in pitch on a modern keyboard, different in meaning and, on instruments with flexible pitch, sometimes different in sound.

sections.heading: The Major Scale: A Pattern of Tones and Semitones
sections.body: Out of the twelve chromatic notes, the major scale selects seven. The selection is defined not by which notes but by the pattern of gaps between them, and that pattern is the definition of the scale: tone, tone, semitone, tone, tone, tone, semitone. In numbers of semitones, the steps are 2, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2, 1, which adds to twelve and so returns exactly to the starting note an octave up. Applied starting from C, the pattern produces C, D, E, F, G, A, B, C, which is precisely the white keys of the piano. This is why C major is taught first: the pattern of black and white keys already encodes the tone-and-semitone structure, with the semitones falling exactly where the white keys are adjacent, between E and F and between B and C. Applied starting from G, the pattern demands G, A, B, C, D, E, then a tone above E, which is F sharp, then a semitone up to G. The key of G major therefore contains one sharp. Applied from F, it demands F, G, A, then a semitone, which is B flat, then C, D, E, F. F major contains one flat. The seven notes have names describing their function, and those names matter far more than they first appear. The first note is the tonic, the home note. The fifth is the dominant, the most powerful note after the tonic and the one that most strongly demands a return to it. The fourth is the subdominant. The third is the mediant, sitting midway between tonic and dominant, and the sixth is the submediant. The second is the supertonic, simply the note above the tonic. The seventh is the leading note, and its name is the most descriptive of all: it sits only a semitone below the tonic and leans upward into it so insistently that a melody stopping on it feels physically unfinished. That semitone gap between the seventh and the eighth degree is the engine of tonal music. Ending a tune on the leading note leaves listeners waiting; resolving it upward by a semitone to the tonic produces the sense of arrival. The other semitone, between the third and fourth degrees, does similar if gentler work. Degrees are conventionally numbered with Roman numerals or Arabic numbers with carets, and musicians think in these numbers rather than in letter names, because the numbers are the same in every key. A melody that goes 1, 5, 6, 5 sounds like the same melody whether it is played in C, in E flat or in B, and that transposability is precisely what makes the scale a useful abstraction rather than a list.

sections.heading: Key Signatures and the Order of Sharps and Flats
sections.body: Writing out every sharp or flat every time it occurs would clutter a score unbearably, so Western notation collects them at the start of each line in a key signature. The key signature is simply a declaration of which notes are permanently altered for the duration, and its contents follow a fixed order that is itself a consequence of stacking fifths. The sharps always appear in this order: F sharp, C sharp, G sharp, D sharp, A sharp, E sharp, B sharp. Each is a fifth above the last. The flats appear in the exact reverse: B flat, E flat, A flat, D flat, G flat, C flat, F flat, each a fifth below the last. Generations of students have learned these with mnemonics, the sharps as Father Charles Goes Down And Ends Battle and the flats as the same sentence read backwards, Battle Ends And Down Goes Charles' Father. Musicians also remember that the flats spell out the word BEAD and then continue G, C, F. Two rules turn a key signature into a key name instantly. For a sharp key, the tonic is a semitone above the last sharp: with four sharps, the last being D sharp, the key is E major. For a flat key, the tonic is the second-to-last flat: with four flats, B flat, E flat, A flat, D flat, the key is A flat major. The single-flat key, F major, has to be memorised because there is no second-to-last flat. Working backwards is just as easy: count the sharps or flats in the key you want by counting its position around the fifths chain. The complete set for major keys runs as follows. With sharps: C has none, G one, D two, A three, E four, B five, F sharp six, C sharp seven. With flats: F has one, B flat two, E flat three, A flat four, D flat five, G flat six, C flat seven. That is fifteen major key signatures for twelve pitch classes, because three pairs overlap: B major and C flat major, F sharp major and G flat major, and C sharp major and D flat major are the same sounds written differently. Accidentals, the sharps, flats and naturals written into the music itself, override the key signature for the remainder of the bar in which they appear and then lapse. This bar-long persistence is a convention that has caught out many sight-readers; a natural sign applied to the first of four Fs in a bar of F sharp major applies to all four. The choice between enharmonic spellings is practical rather than theoretical. Composers pick the spelling with fewer accidentals or the one that makes the harmonic logic clearer on the page, which is why a piece will sit in D flat major rather than C sharp major, five flats being easier to read than seven sharps.

sections.heading: The Circle of Fifths: How to Build It and Read It
sections.body: The circle of fifths arranges all twelve pitch classes around a clock face so that each step clockwise is a perfect fifth up and each step anticlockwise is a perfect fifth down, which is the same as a perfect fourth up. C sits at twelve o'clock. Going clockwise: G, D, A, E, B, F sharp or G flat at the bottom, then D flat, A flat, E flat, B flat, F, and back to C. Its power lies in what the position encodes. Each clockwise step adds exactly one sharp to the key signature; each anticlockwise step adds one flat. C has none, G has one, D has two, and so on around to C sharp with seven. Position on the circle therefore is the key signature, and the diagram replaces a whole table of memorised facts with a single picture. At the bottom, around six o'clock, sharps and flats meet, and those keys are written both ways. The circle also measures musical distance. Adjacent keys share six of their seven notes: C major and G major differ only in that G has F sharp where C has F natural. Keys opposite each other, a tritone apart, share only two. Because moving to a neighbour changes almost nothing, such moves sound smooth and are the commonest modulations in tonal music, while a leap across the circle sounds abrupt. A second ring inside gives the relative minor of each major key, a minor third below the major tonic: A minor inside C, E minor inside G, D minor inside F, each sharing the signature outside it. Reading harmony off the diagram is the everyday use. Any key's two neighbours are its dominant, clockwise, and its subdominant, anticlockwise, so C, G and F sit together as the three primary chords of C major. Progressions moving anticlockwise, such as E to A to D to G to C, are the most common in Western music, because each root is a fifth below the last and every step feels like a resolution.
steps: Draw a circle and write C at the twelve o'clock position; this is the key with no sharps and no flats.
Moving clockwise, count up a perfect fifth each time, seven semitones, and write the result: G, D, A, E, B, and F sharp at six o'clock.
Return to C and move anticlockwise, counting down a perfect fifth, or up a fourth, each time: F, B flat, E flat, A flat, D flat, and G flat, which lands on the same point as F sharp.
Label the number of sharps beside each clockwise position, one for G through six for F sharp, and the number of flats anticlockwise, one for F through six for G flat.
Draw an inner ring and write the relative minor beside each major, a minor third below it: A minor inside C, E minor inside G, D minor inside F, and so on around.
Check the result by naming any key and reading its signature straight off the diagram, confirming it with the rule that a sharp key's tonic sits a semitone above the last sharp.

sections.heading: Minor Keys: Natural, Harmonic and Melodic
sections.body: Minor keys share the twelve chromatic notes and the seven-note principle with major keys but use a different pattern of tones and semitones, and the difference in character is immediate to almost any listener: brighter and more open for major, darker and more inward for minor. The natural minor scale runs tone, semitone, tone, tone, semitone, tone, tone, or in semitones 2, 1, 2, 2, 1, 2, 2. Starting from A this gives A, B, C, D, E, F, G, A, which is again the white keys of the piano. The essential difference from major is the third degree, flattened by a semitone, which is what the ear registers first; the sixth and seventh are also a semitone lower than in the parallel major. Every major key has a relative minor built on its sixth degree, sharing its key signature exactly. C major and A minor share no sharps or flats; G major and E minor share one sharp; F major and D minor share one flat. The relationship is a shared set of notes with a different centre of gravity. Every key also has a parallel minor built on the same tonic: C major and C minor, which have quite different key signatures, none against three flats, but the same home note. Composers exploit both relationships constantly, and the sudden shift from a major to its parallel minor is one of the most reliable expressive gestures in the repertoire. The natural minor has a structural problem, and it is the reason two further forms exist. Its seventh degree sits a whole tone below the tonic rather than a semitone, so it lacks a leading note and the pull toward home is weak. In A minor, the chord built on the fifth degree is E minor, and E minor moving to A minor does not feel like an arrival. The harmonic minor solves this by raising the seventh degree by a semitone: A, B, C, D, E, F, G sharp, A. The dominant chord becomes E major, containing G sharp, and the cadence works. The cost is an awkward gap of three semitones between the sixth and seventh degrees, F to G sharp, which is difficult to sing and sounds distinctly exotic. The melodic minor resolves that in turn by also raising the sixth degree when ascending: A, B, C, D, E, F sharp, G sharp, A going up, and reverting to the natural minor coming down, since the leading note is not needed on the way down. This is the classical convention; in jazz practice the raised form is generally used in both directions and is simply called the melodic minor or jazz minor. In practice composers move freely among all three, choosing whichever degree suits the harmony of the moment, so a minor-key piece is best understood as drawing on a pool of nine available notes rather than a fixed seven.

sections.heading: The Modes: Seven Scales From One Set of Notes
sections.body: Playing the white keys of a piano from C to C produces the major scale. Playing the same white keys from D to D produces a different scale, because the pattern of tones and semitones has rotated. There are seven possible starting points and therefore seven scales, called the modes, and they are among the most useful ideas in practical musicianship. Their names come from ancient Greek regions by way of a medieval misunderstanding, but the labels stuck. Starting on C gives Ionian, which is identical to the major scale. Starting on D gives Dorian: a minor-sounding scale with a raised sixth degree, brighter than natural minor, heard throughout English folk song, in Miles Davis's So What, and in a great deal of modal jazz and rock. Starting on E gives Phrygian: minor with a flattened second, giving a distinctly Spanish or Middle Eastern colour. Starting on F gives Lydian: major with a raised fourth, floating and unresolved, a favourite of film composers for wonder and open space. Starting on G gives Mixolydian: major with a flattened seventh, the sound of a great deal of blues-derived rock and of bagpipe music. Starting on A gives Aeolian, identical to the natural minor. Starting on B gives Locrian, which has both a flattened second and, crucially, a diminished fifth, so the chord on its tonic is unstable and the mode is rarely used as a home key. The important conceptual step is that a mode is not merely a scale run from a different note; it is that scale treated as home. Playing D to D on white keys while a bass line insists on C is simply C major with an unusual melodic starting point. It becomes D Dorian only when D is established as the tonic, typically by a bass note, a drone or a chord built on D. Mode is a matter of tonal centre, and without that centre the whole idea evaporates. Two ways of thinking about modes are both useful. The derivative approach says D Dorian is the notes of C major starting on D, which makes them easy to find on an instrument. The parallel approach says D Dorian is D minor with a raised sixth, which makes their characters easy to compare: relative to a major scale on the same tonic, Lydian raises the fourth, Mixolydian flattens the seventh, Dorian flattens the third and seventh, Aeolian flattens the third, sixth and seventh, Phrygian flattens the second, third, sixth and seventh, and Locrian flattens all of those plus the fifth. Listed that way the modes run from brightest to darkest: Lydian, Ionian, Mixolydian, Dorian, Aeolian, Phrygian, Locrian. Modes dominated European music before roughly 1600, were largely displaced by the major and minor system during the Baroque, and returned emphatically in the twentieth century through folk revival, impressionism, jazz and rock.

sections.heading: Chords Built on Scale Degrees
sections.body: Harmony in tonal music is generated by stacking notes of a scale in thirds, taking every other note, and doing this on each degree in turn produces the chords that belong naturally to a key. This is the bridge between a scale as a set of notes and a key as a working musical system. In C major, building a three-note chord on C takes C, E and G, a C major triad. On D it takes D, F and A, which is D minor, because the gap from D to F is three semitones rather than four. On E it takes E, G and B, E minor. On F, F, A and C, F major. On G, G, B and D, G major. On A, A, C and E, A minor. On B, B, D and F, which is a diminished triad, because both of its intervals are minor thirds and its outer interval is the unstable tritone. The resulting pattern is fixed for every major key: major, minor, minor, major, major, minor, diminished. Musicians label them with Roman numerals, upper case for major and lower case for minor, so a major key gives I, ii, iii, IV, V, vi and vii diminished. In a natural minor key the pattern rotates to i, ii diminished, III, iv, v, VI, VII, and when the seventh is raised for harmonic minor the fifth chord becomes major, V, and the seventh becomes a diminished chord, which is the entire point of raising it. Adding a fourth note, another third above, gives seventh chords, which are the standard vocabulary of jazz and a colouring device in classical music. In a major key these are I major seventh, ii minor seventh, iii minor seventh, IV major seventh, V dominant seventh, vi minor seventh, and vii half diminished. The chord on the fifth degree is the only one that is a dominant seventh, a major triad with a minor seventh on top, and its unique status is the key to functional harmony. It contains both the leading note and the fourth degree, which form a tritone between them, and that tritone is unstable in a highly specific way: the leading note wants to rise a semitone to the tonic and the fourth wants to fall a semitone to the third. Resolving both simultaneously delivers the listener to the tonic chord with unmistakable finality. Chords are commonly grouped by function. The tonic group, I, iii and vi, is stable. The dominant group, V and vii diminished, is maximally unstable and points home. The subdominant or pre-dominant group, IV and ii, is mildly unstable and typically prepares the dominant. An enormous proportion of Western music is built from the cycle tonic, pre-dominant, dominant, tonic, elaborated at every possible scale from a two-bar phrase to a movement lasting half an hour.

sections.heading: Cadences and How a Key Is Established
sections.body: A key does not exist because a key signature says so; it exists because the music persuades the ear that a particular note is home. The persuasion is done chiefly by cadences, the harmonic punctuation marks that end phrases, and by the way the tritone in the dominant chord resolves. The perfect or authentic cadence is V to I, dominant to tonic. In C major that is G to C, and if the dominant is a seventh chord, G7 with its F, the resolution is stronger still. This is the full stop of tonal music, and a piece will usually end with one. When the dominant is in root position, the tonic is in root position, and the tonic note is in the top voice, it is called a perfect authentic cadence and is the most conclusive gesture available. The plagal cadence is IV to I, subdominant to tonic. In C that is F to C, the sound of the sung Amen at the end of a hymn, from which it takes its nickname. It is conclusive but gentler, because it lacks a leading note pushing up into the tonic. The imperfect or half cadence ends on V rather than resolving it, leaving the phrase suspended like a comma or a question mark. Answering phrases in classical melody very often pair a half cadence at the midpoint with a perfect cadence at the end, which is why so many tunes feel like a question followed by an answer. The interrupted or deceptive cadence sets up V and then resolves it to vi instead of I, in C major G to A minor. The ear has been prepared for arrival and is denied it, and composers use this to extend a phrase or to darken a moment at the last instant. Establishing a key at the start of a piece uses much the same machinery. Sounding the tonic chord does some of the work, but the strongest evidence is a dominant that resolves to it, because the dominant seventh chord of a given key occurs naturally in no other major key; its combination of a leading note and a fourth degree is unique. This is why two or three chords are usually enough for a listener to know exactly where they are. Two further factors matter and are often underestimated. The first is repetition and metrical placement: whatever note or chord falls on strong beats and returns most often will be heard as home almost regardless of theory. The second is the bass. A pedal note held in the bass will assert itself as the tonal centre against a good deal of contradicting harmony above it, which is why drones in folk and early music are such an efficient way of establishing a mode.

sections.heading: Modulation: Moving From One Key to Another
sections.body: A piece that stays in one key for twenty minutes becomes wearing, and the standard solution is modulation, a genuine change of tonal centre rather than a passing chromatic note. Modulation is the main source of large-scale structure in classical music, and the circle of fifths is the map that governs it. The keys that a piece modulates to most easily are its closest neighbours, meaning those whose key signatures differ by no more than one sharp or flat. For C major these are G major, its dominant; F major, its subdominant; A minor, its relative minor; and the relative minors of the neighbours, E minor and D minor. Between them these five keys account for the overwhelming majority of modulations in the common-practice repertoire. Sonata form in the eighteenth century was built on precisely this principle: a major-key movement typically moves to the dominant for its second theme and returns to the tonic for the recapitulation, while a minor-key movement usually goes to the relative major. The commonest technique is the pivot chord. Because neighbouring keys share six of seven notes, they also share several chords, and a shared chord can be introduced as belonging to the old key and then reinterpreted as belonging to the new. Moving from C major to G major, the chord of C is I in the old key and IV in the new; the chord of A minor is vi in the old key and ii in the new. The pivot is sounded, then immediately followed by the new key's dominant, D major or D7, resolving to G. The listener's sense of home slides across without a seam. This is sometimes called common-chord modulation, and it is the default of the classical style. Other techniques are blunter and often more striking. Direct modulation simply shifts, without preparation, most familiarly the upward semitone or tone lurch in the last chorus of a pop song. Chromatic modulation alters a note of a chord by a semitone to turn it into a chord of the new key. Enharmonic modulation exploits chords whose spelling is ambiguous, above all the diminished seventh chord, which divides the octave into four equal minor thirds and can therefore resolve into any of four keys, and the augmented sixth chords, which sound identical to dominant sevenths and can be reinterpreted as such. These allow a composer to travel to a remote key in a single chord, a device Schubert and Beethoven both used to startling effect. Judging when a modulation has actually happened is a real analytical skill, and the honest answer is that it is a matter of degree rather than a switch. A single chord from another key is a tonicisation, a brief nod, not a modulation. A modulation proper requires that the new key be confirmed, usually by a cadence in it and by enough time spent there for the ear to accept the new home.

sections.heading: Tuning and Temperament: Why the Circle Nearly Fails to Close
sections.body: The circle of fifths is drawn as a closed loop, but the fifths that generate it do not actually close, and the history of how musicians handled that gap is the history of tuning. Twelve pure fifths overshoot seven octaves by the Pythagorean comma, about 23.5 cents, roughly a quarter of a semitone and unmistakably out of tune when heard. Pythagorean tuning, used through much of the Middle Ages, kept every fifth pure and dumped the entire error into one interval, producing a howling fifth known as the wolf, usually placed between G sharp and E flat where it would be least used. Fifths and fourths were beautiful; major thirds, at a ratio of 81:64 rather than the pure 5:4, were about 22 cents sharp and sounded harsh, which is one reason medieval music treated thirds as dissonances. As thirds became central to Renaissance harmony, quarter-comma meantone tuning took over. It deliberately flattened each fifth by about 5.4 cents, a quarter of a different small discrepancy called the syntonic comma, so that four fifths would land on a pure major third. Thirds became gorgeous, most keys sounded excellent, and a single dreadful wolf fifth remained, which meant the usable keys were limited to those with few sharps and flats. This constraint is audible in the repertoire: composers of the period simply did not write in remote keys. The well temperaments of the late seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, associated with Andreas Werckmeister and others, distributed the error unevenly so that every key was usable but each had its own colour, the common keys being purer and the remote ones spicier. Johann Sebastian Bach's Das Wohltemperirte Clavier of 1722, with a prelude and fugue in every major and minor key, was a demonstration of exactly this possibility. It is a persistent and incorrect popular claim that Bach's title means equal temperament; the evidence points to an unequal well temperament, though which one remains genuinely disputed among scholars. Equal temperament divides the octave into twelve identical semitones, each a frequency ratio of the twelfth root of two, about 1.05946. Every fifth is 700 cents, two cents flat of pure, which is essentially inaudible. Every major third is 400 cents against a pure 386, about 14 cents sharp, which is audible as a slight beating but is accepted as the price of the system. All keys become exactly equivalent, transposition becomes trivial, and modulation anywhere becomes free. It became the standard for pianos through the nineteenth century. Something real was lost. In equal temperament no interval except the octave is pure, and the individual character of keys, taken seriously by composers into the Romantic era, disappears. Unaccompanied choirs, string quartets and barbershop singers routinely drift toward pure intervals because they sound better, which is why a good a cappella group can end a piece measurably sharp or flat of where it started.

sections.heading: Scales Beyond Major and Minor
sections.body: The seven-note major and minor scales dominate Western art and popular music, but they are a small part of what human beings actually sing and play, and several other scales are so widely used that they belong in any working understanding. The major pentatonic scale takes five notes, degrees 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6, so in C that is C, D, E, G, A. It omits the fourth and seventh, which are precisely the two notes involved in the semitone tensions, so nothing in it clashes and any note can be played over any chord of the key. It is the black keys of the piano transposed, and it appears independently in Chinese, Scottish, west African, Andean and Appalachian traditions, almost certainly because it can be generated by four steps of stacked fifths and because its lack of semitones makes it forgiving. The minor pentatonic, degrees 1, flat 3, 4, 5, flat 7, is the backbone of blues, rock and a vast amount of guitar improvisation. The blues scale adds a flattened fifth to the minor pentatonic as a passing note, giving 1, flat 3, 4, flat 5, 5, flat 7. It is a written approximation of something notation cannot really capture: the blue notes of African American vocal practice sit between the notated pitches, bent and inflected, and the piano's fixed pitches can only gesture at them. Symmetrical scales divide the octave evenly and therefore have no single tonic. The whole-tone scale uses six notes a whole tone apart, has no semitones and no perfect fifth, and sounds weightless and directionless, which is exactly why Debussy used it for shimmering, unanchored textures. The octatonic or diminished scale alternates whole tones and semitones for eight notes, and was exploited systematically by Rimsky-Korsakov, Stravinsky and Messiaen. The chromatic scale itself, using all twelve, underlies the twelve-tone method Arnold Schoenberg formulated around 1921, which deliberately abolished the hierarchy that makes a key. Other traditions organise pitch quite differently, and it is worth being careful not to describe them merely as variants of Western practice. The Indian classical system uses ragas, which specify not only a set of pitches but characteristic phrases, ornaments, ascending and descending forms, emphasis notes and often a time of day, and its microtonal shrutis do not map onto twelve equal semitones. Arabic and Turkish maqam systems use quarter-tone-like intervals that a piano cannot play at all. Indonesian gamelan uses slendro and pelog tunings that vary from one ensemble to the next by design, so that each gamelan has its own voice. Each of these is a complete system with its own logic, not an approximation of the major scale.

sections.heading: Using It: Transposition, Instruments and Practical Fluency
sections.body: Theory earns its keep when it makes practical tasks quick, and scales, keys and the circle of fifths are unusually productive in this respect. Transposition is the clearest case. Because a melody is defined by scale degrees rather than by letter names, moving a song into a singable key is a matter of shifting every degree by the same amount. A song in G whose chords are G, E minor, C and D is I, vi, IV, V; a singer who needs it three semitones lower puts it into E, and the chords become E, C sharp minor, A and B. Working in numbers rather than letters makes this an instant operation rather than an arithmetic exercise, and it is why professional accompanists think in Roman numerals or in the Nashville number system. Transposing instruments make the same skill compulsory in ensembles. A B flat clarinet or trumpet sounds a whole tone lower than written, so their parts are notated a whole tone higher than concert pitch and carry a key signature two sharps further round the circle: when the orchestra is in concert C, the clarinet reads D major. An E flat alto saxophone sounds a major sixth lower than written and so reads three sharps further round; an F horn sounds a perfect fifth lower and reads one sharp further. Each of these is simply a fixed rotation around the circle of fifths. For instrumentalists, practising scales is not an arbitrary ritual. It builds the physical patterns in which nearly all tonal melody is written, teaches the hand where the semitones fall in each key, and links the ear to the fingers. A defensible practice order follows the circle rather than the alphabet: learn C, then G, then D, adding one sharp at a time, and separately C, F, B flat, adding one flat, so that each new key differs from the last by a single note. On guitar and other fretted instruments the same shape moves bodily up the neck, so one fingering pattern serves all twelve keys, which is both an enormous convenience and a reason many guitarists never learn to name what they are playing. For songwriters and improvisers the circle offers a fast route to plausible harmony. Choose a key, take its seven diatonic chords, and any sequence of them will function; move anticlockwise around the circle for the strongest-sounding progressions; borrow a chord from the parallel minor for colour, such as using an F minor chord in the key of C. And when a progression sounds wrong, the diagnosis is usually that a chord has been taken from a key more than one step away on the circle without being prepared.

sections.heading: Common Confusions, Limits and When the Theory Does Not Fit
sections.body: Several persistent misunderstandings cause more trouble than genuine difficulty in this subject, and naming them plainly saves a great deal of time. The first is treating theory as a set of rules that music must obey. It is not. Music theory is descriptive, an account of the patterns that a particular body of music happens to use, mostly European art music between about 1650 and 1900 plus the popular music descended from it. When a piece does not fit, the piece is not wrong. Modal folk song, blues, much film music and most non-Western traditions routinely violate common-practice rules and are none the worse for it. The second is confusing a key signature with a key. Two sharps means the piece uses F sharp and C sharp; it does not by itself say whether the key is D major or B minor, and it does not prevent the music from being in E Dorian or A Mixolydian, both of which use the same two sharps. Deciding the actual key requires listening for which note behaves like home, checking the final chord, and looking for accidentals that signal a raised leading note in a minor key. The third is assuming enharmonic equivalents are simply interchangeable. On a piano, C sharp and D flat are the same key, but they are not the same musical idea: a C sharp is normally rising toward D, a D flat falling toward C, and the choice is what makes a passage legible. On a violin, a trombone or in a voice, they may be genuinely different pitches, a performer often placing a leading note slightly high to intensify its pull. The fourth is over-trusting the circle of fifths. It is a map of one kind of distance, the diatonic kind. It says nothing useful about chromatic mediant relationships, about the equal divisions of the octave that late Romantic and film composers favour, or about music organised by timbre, rhythm or texture rather than by harmony. A fifth confusion, and the most common among beginners, is expecting theory to generate music. Knowing every key signature will not produce a melody, and a great deal of memorably good music uses only three chords. The value of the framework is that it makes what you hear analysable, makes what you imagine writable, and makes communication with other musicians efficient. When something does not fit, the productive response is a short checklist: identify the actual tonal centre by ear rather than from the signature; test whether the passage is modal rather than major or minor; check for borrowed chords from the parallel key; consider whether a modulation has occurred and to where on the circle; and, if none of these explains it, accept that the music may be operating by principles this system was never built to describe.

guides.title: Intervals and How to Hear Them
guides.summary: What a musical interval is, the physics and naming system behind it, and a practical method for training your ear to identify intervals reliably by sound alone.

sections.heading: What an Interval Is and Why Everything Rests on It
sections.body:
An interval is the distance in pitch between two notes. That is the whole definition, and it sounds almost too simple to build a discipline on, yet essentially all of Western music theory and most practical musicianship is constructed from it. A melody is a sequence of intervals. A chord is a stack of them. A scale is a particular pattern of them. Harmony is the study of how they combine and move. When a musician says a piece has been transposed, they mean every pitch has changed but every interval has stayed the same, and the reason the tune is still recognisable is that the listener was never hearing the pitches in the first place. They were hearing the relationships.

This is the central and slightly startling fact about human musical perception. Play "Happy Birthday" starting on C and then starting on F sharp, and almost everyone hears the same tune, despite not one note being shared between the two versions. The information that carries the melody is entirely relational. Very few people, perhaps one in ten thousand in the general Western population, possess absolute pitch, the ability to name a note without reference to another, and even they generally use relative hearing to follow music. Everyone else, including the overwhelming majority of professional musicians, works from intervals.

The practical consequences run through every part of musicianship. A singer holding a line in a choir is not finding an absolute frequency; they are measuring a distance from the note beside them. A guitarist tuning by ear is matching intervals. A jazz player transcribing a solo hears a shape and converts it to intervals before converting it to notes. A composer imagining a melody is manipulating intervals in their head. And someone learning to play by ear is, in almost all cases, blocked not by their instrument but by their inability to name the distances they are hearing.

The good news is that interval recognition is a trainable skill, and unusually among musical abilities it is trainable at any age. Absolute pitch appears to require exposure during a critical period in early childhood, roughly before the age of six or seven, and adults who attempt to acquire it generally achieve only limited, effortful results. Relative pitch has no such restriction. Adults who practise systematically routinely go from being unable to distinguish a third from a fifth to reliable identification within a few months. The obstacle is not talent but method, and most people who conclude they are tone deaf have simply never been shown how the training actually works.

A small proportion of people do have genuine congenital amusia, a neurological condition affecting perhaps 1.5 to 4 per cent of the population, in which fine pitch discrimination is genuinely impaired. But it is far rarer than the number who describe themselves that way, and it is worth knowing that self-diagnosis in this area is almost always wrong.

sections.heading: Naming Intervals: Number and Quality
sections.body:
Every interval name in Western music has two parts: a number and a quality. The number describes how far apart the notes are counted by letter name, and the quality refines that into an exact distance in semitones.

The number is counted inclusively, which is the first thing that trips people up. From C to E, you count C, D, E, which is three letters, so the interval is a third, even though it spans only two steps. From C to G you count C, D, E, F, G, which is five letters, so it is a fifth. From C up to the next C you count eight, hence octave, from the Latin for eighth. This inclusive counting is a historical inheritance and it means the arithmetic never quite behaves: a third plus a third makes a fifth, not a sixth, because the shared note is counted twice.

Critically, the number depends on the letter names written, not on the sound. C to E flat and C to D sharp produce the same pitch on a piano, but the first is a third, because C to E spans three letters, and the second is a second, because C to D spans two. They are enharmonic equivalents, identical in sound and different in spelling and function.

The quality distinguishes the varieties that share a number. Four qualities are in general use: perfect, major, minor, augmented and diminished, giving five terms in total. Perfect applies only to unisons, fourths, fifths and octaves. Major and minor apply only to seconds, thirds, sixths and sevenths. Every interval type can additionally be augmented, meaning one semitone wider than perfect or major, or diminished, meaning one semitone narrower than perfect or minor.

The full ladder within an octave, measured in semitones from the lower note, runs as follows: perfect unison is 0, minor second is 1, major second is 2, minor third is 3, major third is 4, perfect fourth is 5, augmented fourth or diminished fifth is 6, perfect fifth is 7, minor sixth is 8, major sixth is 9, minor seventh is 10, major seventh is 11, and perfect octave is 12.

A reliable way to derive quality without memorising the table is to use the major scale of the lower note. Every interval from the tonic up to a note of its own major scale is either perfect or major: C to D is a major second because D is in C major, C to F is a perfect fourth because F is in C major. If the upper note is one semitone lower than the scale note, a major becomes minor and a perfect becomes diminished. One semitone higher and either becomes augmented. This single procedure handles every case, including awkward spellings such as C to B double flat, which is a diminished seventh, and it works from any starting note once you know your scales.

sections.heading: The Physics: Frequency Ratios and the Harmonic Series
sections.body:
Intervals are not arbitrary cultural conventions; they sit on top of physical acoustics, and the reason certain distances recur in unrelated musical traditions is that they are built into how sound works.

Pitch corresponds to frequency, measured in hertz, or cycles per second. The reference pitch A above middle C is conventionally 440 Hz, though this has varied historically and orchestras today commonly tune to 440, 442 or 443. What the ear perceives as an interval is not a difference in frequency but a ratio. The octave above A440 is 880 Hz, and the octave above that is 1760; the differences are 440 and 880, but the ratio is 2:1 in both cases, and both sound like the same interval. Pitch perception is logarithmic, which is why musical notation uses evenly spaced staff positions for what are geometrically increasing frequencies.

The simplest ratios come from the harmonic series, which is the set of frequencies a vibrating string or air column naturally produces. A string tuned to 100 Hz vibrates not only along its whole length but simultaneously in halves, thirds, quarters and so on, producing partials at 200, 300, 400, 500, 600, 700 Hz and upward, all integer multiples of the fundamental. Every note from a violin, a voice, a trumpet or a guitar contains this stack, and the relative strength of the partials is what makes a clarinet sound different from an oboe playing the same pitch.

The intervals between adjacent harmonics are precisely the intervals of music. Harmonic 1 to 2 is 2:1, the octave. Harmonic 2 to 3 is 3:2, the perfect fifth. Harmonic 3 to 4 is 4:3, the perfect fourth. Harmonic 4 to 5 is 5:4, the major third. Harmonic 5 to 6 is 6:5, the minor third. Continue and you get 5:3 for the major sixth, 8:5 for the minor sixth, 15:8 for the major seventh, 16:15 for the minor second, and 9:8 for the major second. This is not a coincidence imposed on nature; the intervals were discovered by listening to strings and pipes, and the ratios were found afterward.

Pythagoras, or more accurately the Pythagorean tradition of the sixth century BCE, is credited with establishing that consonant intervals correspond to simple whole-number ratios, demonstrated on a monochord, a single string with a movable bridge. Stop the string exactly halfway and the pitch rises an octave; at two-thirds of its length, a fifth; at three-quarters, a fourth. The observation that musical beauty and simple arithmetic coincide was, for the Pythagoreans, evidence of cosmic order, and it remained the intellectual foundation of European music theory for two thousand years.

One practical demonstration is available on any stringed instrument. Touch a guitar string lightly exactly halfway along and pluck it: the fundamental is suppressed and the second harmonic sounds, an octave above. Touch at a third of the length and you get the twelfth, an octave plus a fifth. These are the natural harmonics, and they are audible proof that the intervals are physically present in a single vibrating string rather than imposed on it.

sections.heading: Consonance, Dissonance and Why Some Intervals Sound Sweet
sections.body:
Some intervals sound smooth and stable, others rough and unsettled, and the distinction is called consonance and dissonance. Explaining why has occupied theorists for centuries, and the modern answer combines two mechanisms, one acoustic and one cultural.

The acoustic mechanism is roughness from interfering partials, worked out substantially by Hermann von Helmholtz in his 1863 work On the Sensations of Tone and refined by Reinier Plomp and Willem Levelt in 1965. When two tones sound together, all their harmonics sound together too. If two partials are close in frequency but not identical, they interfere and produce beating, a periodic wobble in loudness at a rate equal to the frequency difference. Slow beating, below about 6 Hz, is heard as a pleasant tremor. Beating in the range of roughly 15 to 40 Hz is heard as roughness or harshness. Very widely separated partials do not interfere at all.

The critical band, the region of the inner ear within which two frequencies compete, sets the scale. Plomp and Levelt found that perceived dissonance peaks when two partials are separated by about a quarter of a critical bandwidth. Simple frequency ratios put many partials exactly on top of each other, where they reinforce rather than interfere; complex ratios scatter them into the roughness zone.

A worked example makes this concrete and also explains a practical fact about pianos. Take A at 440 Hz and the E above it. In equal temperament that E is 659.26 Hz. The third harmonic of the A is 1320 Hz; the second harmonic of the E is 1318.51 Hz. They beat at about 1.5 times per second, which is slow enough to be almost imperceptible, and the fifth sounds clean. Now take the C sharp above A440, which in equal temperament is 554.37 Hz. The fifth harmonic of the A is 2200 Hz; the fourth harmonic of the C sharp is 2217.5 Hz. These beat about 17.5 times per second, squarely in the roughness zone, which is why equal-tempered major thirds have a faint but genuine buzz that many listeners notice once it is pointed out.

The cultural mechanism is that consonance judgements are also learned. The perfect fourth was treated as a consonance in medieval organum and later reclassified as a dissonance requiring resolution when it appeared above the bass. The major third was regarded with suspicion in early medieval theory and became the foundation of triadic harmony by the Renaissance. Studies comparing listeners across cultures, including a much-discussed 2016 study of the Tsimané people of the Bolivian Amazon, found weak or absent preference for consonant over dissonant intervals in populations with limited exposure to Western harmony, which suggests the acoustic effect is real but the aesthetic preference is substantially acquired. The honest position is that both mechanisms contribute and their relative weight remains genuinely contested.

sections.heading: Tuning Systems and the Comma Problem
sections.body:
If simple ratios sound best, the obvious approach is to tune every interval to its pure ratio. This turns out to be impossible, and the reason is one of the most consequential facts in the history of music.

Build a series of pure perfect fifths, each 3:2, starting from C: C, G, D, A, E, B, F sharp, C sharp, G sharp, D sharp, A sharp, E sharp. Twelve fifths should return you to C, seven octaves higher. Do the arithmetic and it does not. Twelve fifths multiply to (3/2) raised to the twelfth power, which is 129.746. Seven octaves is 2 to the seventh, which is 128. The mismatch, 531441 divided by 524288, equals 1.013643, and it is called the Pythagorean comma. It amounts to about 23.5 cents, roughly a quarter of a semitone, which is unmistakably out of tune.

A second, independent mismatch afflicts thirds. Four pure fifths stacked give a ratio of 5.0625, whereas two octaves plus a pure major third gives exactly 5. The discrepancy, 81 to 80, is the syntonic comma, about 21.5 cents. There is no way to arrange twelve fixed pitches so that all fifths and all thirds are pure. The problem is arithmetic, not craftsmanship, and every tuning system in history is a different compromise about where to hide the error.

Pythagorean tuning keeps all fifths pure and dumps the entire comma into one interval, the so-called wolf fifth, which is unusable. Its thirds are noticeably wide at about 408 cents. Quarter-comma meantone, dominant in Europe from roughly the sixteenth to the eighteenth centuries, narrows each fifth by a quarter of a syntonic comma to about 696.6 cents, which makes major thirds exactly pure at 386.3 cents. It sounds beautiful in the keys it serves and progressively worse as you move round the circle, which is precisely why music of that era stays close to home harmonically. Well temperaments, of which Werckmeister's schemes from 1681 are the best known, distribute the error unevenly so that every key is playable but each has a distinct character.

Equal temperament divides the octave into twelve exactly equal steps, each a ratio of the twelfth root of two, approximately 1.059463. Every key sounds identical, modulation anywhere becomes free, and every interval except the octave is slightly wrong. The fifth is 700 cents against a pure 702, only two cents narrow and essentially undetectable. The major third is 400 cents against a pure 386.3, nearly fourteen cents sharp, which is the compromise we all live with. It became standard in the nineteenth century, though it is a persistent myth that Bach's Well-Tempered Clavier of 1722 demands it; well-tempered meant playable in all keys, not equal, and what Bach actually used remains genuinely unsettled.

Unfretted string players and singers do not obey any of this and adjust intervals continuously by ear.

sections.heading: Cents, Measurement and the Limits of Hearing
sections.body:
To compare tuning systems and to measure how accurate a performance is, musicians need a unit finer than the semitone. That unit is the cent, proposed by Alexander Ellis in the 1880s, defined so that one equal-tempered semitone contains exactly 100 cents and an octave contains 1200.

Because pitch is logarithmic, converting a frequency ratio to cents requires a logarithm. The formula is that the interval in cents equals 1200 multiplied by the base-two logarithm of the ratio of the two frequencies. Checking it on the octave, the ratio is 2, the base-two logarithm of 2 is 1, and the result is 1200 cents, as required. For the pure perfect fifth the ratio is 1.5, whose base-two logarithm is 0.58496, giving 701.955 cents. For the pure major third the ratio is 1.25, giving 386.31 cents. If your calculator lacks a base-two logarithm, divide the natural or common logarithm of the ratio by the corresponding logarithm of 2.

Running the pure ratios through this gives a table worth internalising, with the equal-tempered value alongside: minor second 16:15 is 111.7 against 100, major second 9:8 is 203.9 against 200, minor third 6:5 is 315.6 against 300, major third 5:4 is 386.3 against 400, perfect fourth 4:3 is 498.0 against 500, tritone 45:32 is 590.2 against 600, perfect fifth 3:2 is 702.0 against 700, minor sixth 8:5 is 813.7 against 800, major sixth 5:3 is 884.4 against 900, minor seventh 16:9 is 996.1 against 1000, and major seventh 15:8 is 1088.3 against 1100.

The pattern is instructive. Fourths and fifths are within two cents of pure, which is why equal temperament works at all. Thirds and sixths are out by thirteen to sixteen cents, which is audible to a trained ear as beating but which most listeners accept as normal because they have heard nothing else.

How fine is human pitch discrimination? For two tones played in succession in the middle of the range, trained listeners can typically detect a difference of around 5 to 6 cents, and some do better; untrained listeners are nearer 10 to 20. Discrimination worsens at very low and very high frequencies, with short notes, and with complex or noisy timbres. For two tones played simultaneously, sensitivity is far greater, because beating is easy to hear even when the pitch difference is not: a piano tuner can set an interval to within one or two cents by counting beats per second, a skill that depends on rhythm rather than pitch perception. This is why tuning by ear is a different and in some ways easier task than identifying a pitch by ear.

Cents are also the unit in which performance intonation is discussed. String quartets and choirs routinely drift from equal temperament by ten to twenty cents in the direction of pure intervals, sharpening leading notes and lowering thirds in major chords, and this is generally heard as good intonation rather than error. A tuner reading in cents is therefore a useful diagnostic tool and a poor arbiter of musical correctness.

sections.heading: The Intervals One by One: Unison Through Fourth
sections.body:
Learning intervals means acquiring a distinct character for each, and the characters are worth describing individually because they are not interchangeable.

The perfect unison, 0 semitones, is two instances of the same pitch. It sounds like a single note with a thickened tone, and detecting whether two players are in unison or slightly apart is the fundamental tuning skill: any mistuning produces beating at the difference frequency.

The minor second, 1 semitone, ratio 16:15, is the smallest interval in standard Western music and the most dissonant. Played together the two notes grind audibly. It is the interval of tension, menace and unresolved pressure, and its use as the two-note shark motif in the 1975 film Jaws is probably the most efficient demonstration in popular culture. In melody it is the step between the leading note and the tonic, the half-step that gives Western tonality its pull.

The major second, 2 semitones, ratio 9:8, is the ordinary step of the major scale, the interval you move by when you sing "Hap-py" at the start of Happy Birthday. Sounded together it is mildly dissonant, gentler than the minor second, and it is the characteristic sound of suspended and added-second harmony.

The minor third, 3 semitones, ratio 6:5, is the first genuinely consonant interval and the one most immediately associated with sadness in Western listeners, though that association is cultural rather than acoustic. It is the interval that opens Greensleeves and the descending gap in the Beatles' "Hey Jude". It defines the minor triad.

The major third, 4 semitones, ratio 5:4, is the brightest consonance and the defining interval of the major triad, and therefore of a very large share of all Western music. It is the leap in "When the Saints Go Marching In" between the first and second notes. Because equal temperament makes it fourteen cents sharp, it is also the interval where the compromise of modern tuning is most audible.

The perfect fourth, 5 semitones, ratio 4:3, is stable but oddly ambiguous: consonant against a note above it and unstable against the bass, which is why it has moved in and out of the consonant category across history. It is the opening leap of Wagner's Bridal Chorus and of "Amazing Grace", and it is the interval by which most of a guitar is tuned. Stacked in fourths rather than thirds, it produces the open, modern quartal harmony of much twentieth-century jazz.

Two general observations apply across this lower half of the octave. First, the small intervals, the seconds, are the ones the ear finds hardest to place in a melody, because a step of one or two semitones is easily heard as ordinary scalewise motion rather than as a distinct leap; the larger the interval, the more it announces itself. Second, the difference between major and minor forms of the same number, a single semitone, is the most emotionally loaded distinction in Western music and simultaneously the one most often confused by beginners. Practising major against minor pairs directly, third against third and sixth against sixth, is more productive than practising each alone, because the ear learns fastest by contrast.

sections.heading: The Intervals One by One: Tritone Through Octave
sections.body:
The tritone, 6 semitones, sits exactly halfway through the octave and is the most unusual interval in the system. Its name comes from its span of three whole tones, and it appears as either an augmented fourth or a diminished fifth depending on spelling and function, the two being enharmonically identical on a keyboard but harmonically distinct. Its just ratio is disputed because it has no simple one: 45:32 at 590 cents and 7:5 at 583 are both used. It is uniquely unstable, it inverts to itself, and it is the interval that makes a dominant seventh chord demand resolution. It is worth correcting a widely repeated myth: the medieval phrase mi contra fa est diabolus in musica, the devil in music, was a practical rule about singing awkward melodic leaps within the hexachord system, not a church ban on the interval, and no evidence supports the story that using it was punishable. The theme from The Simpsons and the word "Ma-ri-a" in Bernstein's West Side Story both open with one.

The perfect fifth, 7 semitones, ratio 3:2, is the most consonant interval after the octave and the structural backbone of Western harmony. It opens "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star" and the main theme of Star Wars. Its acoustic purity is why it survives equal temperament almost untouched and why open fifths, with no third to define major or minor, sound archaic and elemental.

The minor sixth, 8 semitones, ratio 8:5, is the inversion of the major third and carries a yearning, romantic quality; the ascending leap in the theme from the film Love Story is a standard reference. The major sixth, 9 semitones, ratio 5:3, is the inversion of the minor third and sounds open and warm; "My Bonnie Lies Over the Ocean" opens with one.

The minor seventh, 10 semitones, is the interval of the dominant seventh chord and the blues, ambiguous and forward-leaning. "There's a place for us" at the opening of Bernstein's "Somewhere" is the standard ascending reference, as is the original Star Trek theme. Its tuning is genuinely contested: the Pythagorean 16:9 at 996 cents and the harmonic seventh 7:4 at 969 cents are meaningfully different, and barbershop singers and brass players routinely find the flatter version by ear because it locks acoustically.

The major seventh, 11 semitones, ratio 15:8, is a semitone below the octave and sounds sharply dissonant when sounded together, yet luminous when spread out in jazz voicings. The chorus of a-ha's "Take On Me" leaps one.

The perfect octave, 12 semitones, ratio 2:1, is so consonant that most listeners hear the two notes as the same note in two places, a phenomenon called octave equivalence, which underlies the entire practice of naming pitches with only seven letters. "Somewhere Over the Rainbow" begins with one.

sections.heading: Compound Intervals, Inversion and Enharmonic Spelling
sections.body:
Three operations extend the basic vocabulary and are worth handling explicitly, because each has a small trap in it.

Compound intervals are those larger than an octave. A ninth is an octave plus a second, a tenth an octave plus a third, an eleventh an octave plus a fourth, a thirteenth an octave plus a sixth. The arithmetic rule is that you subtract seven, not eight, to find the simple equivalent, because of inclusive counting: a thirteenth minus seven is a sixth. Quality carries over unchanged, so a major thirteenth is an octave plus a major sixth. In practice, compound intervals sound like their simple forms with more air and less roughness, since spreading the notes apart removes the partials from each other's critical bands, which is exactly why a close-voiced minor second is unbearable and a minor ninth is merely spicy. Jazz chord symbols use compound numbers deliberately to indicate register: a chord written as a thirteenth implies the note is up in the extension, not sitting next to the third.

Inversion means moving the lower note up an octave, or the upper note down, so that the two swap positions. Two rules govern it, and both are exact. The numbers of an interval and its inversion always sum to nine: a third inverts to a sixth, a fourth to a fifth, a second to a seventh, a unison to an octave. Again the oddity is inclusive counting. And the qualities swap: major becomes minor, minor becomes major, augmented becomes diminished, diminished becomes augmented, and perfect stays perfect. So a major third inverts to a minor sixth, an augmented fourth to a diminished fifth, and a perfect fifth to a perfect fourth. This is not merely bookkeeping; it means learning one interval effectively teaches you its partner, and it is why a well-designed practice regime pairs them.

Enharmonic spelling is the trap that catches even fluent musicians. C to F sharp and C to G flat sound identical on a keyboard, but the first is an augmented fourth and the second a diminished fifth, and they behave differently: the augmented fourth tends to expand outward to a sixth, the diminished fifth to contract inward to a third. Spelling encodes intention. In a dominant seventh chord on G, the tritone between B and F is written that way because B is a leading note that rises and F is a seventh that falls. Rewriting F as E sharp would be technically the same sound and would misrepresent the music entirely.

The double accidentals that arise from strict spelling look intimidating and are simply consequences of the rules. A diminished seventh chord built on C sharp contains B double flat, because the interval from C sharp to that note must be a seventh, spanning seven letters, and only a B of some kind will do. Once the rule is understood the notation stops looking perverse.

sections.heading: Melodic and Harmonic Intervals Are Different Skills
sections.body:
An interval can be played as two notes in succession, which is called melodic, or as two notes together, which is called harmonic. These sound different, are recognised by different perceptual routes, and must be trained separately. Many learners plateau because they practise only one and assume the other will follow.

Melodic intervals are heard as a movement, a leap of a certain size in a certain direction. The perceptual cue is essentially spatial: the ear tracks a trajectory. This is the form in which most song-reference training works, because songs are melodies. It is also the form that matters for transcribing a tune, following a vocal line, or singing at sight.

Melodic intervals also come in two directions, and ascending and descending are genuinely distinct skills. Most people find ascending easier at first, largely because most reference songs are ascending. Descending intervals frequently need their own reference set and their own practice; a learner who is confident on an ascending major sixth may be helpless on a descending one. Direction sensitivity is often the largest single gap in a partially trained ear.

Harmonic intervals are heard as a single composite sound with a texture: smooth, rough, hollow, sweet, buzzing. The cue is timbral rather than spatial, and the mechanism is the interference of partials. Recognising them is closer to recognising a colour than a distance. This is the form that matters for identifying chords, tuning, and hearing inner voices in a texture. A useful technique for beginners is to break a harmonic interval mentally into its melodic form by imagining the lower note moving to the upper, but this is a scaffold to be discarded, because it is slow and it fails on dense chords.

Register changes the difficulty of both. Intervals in the middle of the piano, roughly two octaves either side of middle C, are easiest. Very low intervals become muddy because the partials of the lower note crowd into the same critical band, which is precisely why arrangers avoid close intervals in the bass and why a major third sounds acceptable in the treble and thick in the low register. Very high intervals lose their sense of harmonic identity as the ear's frequency resolution declines.

Timbre matters too. A piano gives a clean, decaying tone with a strong harmonic series and is the standard training instrument. A pure sine tone, which has no harmonics at all, is much harder to work with because the roughness cues vanish, and consonance judgements on sine tones are notably weaker in experiments. A distorted electric guitar or a heavily processed synthesiser adds partials that do not belong to the natural series and can make an interval nearly unidentifiable. Train on ordinary instrumental timbres first.

sections.heading: The Song-Reference Method and Its Limits
sections.body:
The standard beginner technique for interval recognition is to attach each interval to the opening of a familiar song, so that hearing the interval triggers the tune and the tune supplies the name. It works, it is the fastest way to get from nothing to functional recognition, and it has a ceiling that everyone eventually hits.

A workable ascending set, which most teachers use some version of, runs roughly: minor second, the two-note shark motif from Jaws; major second, "Hap-py Birthday"; minor third, the opening of Greensleeves; major third, "Oh, when the saints"; perfect fourth, the Bridal Chorus, "Here comes the bride"; tritone, the opening of The Simpsons theme or "Ma-ri-a"; perfect fifth, "Twinkle, twinkle" or the Star Wars main theme; minor sixth, the theme from Love Story; major sixth, "My Bon-nie lies over the ocean"; minor seventh, "There's a place for us" from Somewhere, or the original Star Trek theme; major seventh, the chorus leap in "Take On Me"; octave, "Some-where over the rainbow".

A descending set is separately required and is where most published lists get thin. Widely used ones include: descending minor second, the opening of Für Elise; descending major second, "Mary Had a Little Lamb" or the first two notes of "Yesterday"; descending minor third, "Hey Jude"; descending major third, the opening motif of Beethoven's Fifth Symphony or "Swing Low, Sweet Chariot"; descending perfect fifth, "The Flintstones" theme.

Two honest cautions apply. First, these references only work if you actually know the songs, and cultural familiarity varies enormously; a list assembled for one generation or country may be useless for another. The correct response is to build your own list from music you know intimately, checking each candidate on an instrument to be sure the interval really is what you think. A reference you half-remember is worse than none.

Second, and more fundamentally, the song method is a lookup table, and lookup is slow. Recognising an interval by recalling a song, humming it internally and comparing takes on the order of a second or two, which is far too slow for real-time transcription, sight-singing or hearing inner voices in a chord. It also fails in context: an interval embedded in a melody, harmonised, or played at speed does not present cleanly enough to match against a remembered opening.

The method is therefore best understood as scaffolding. Use it to get started, use it deliberately and thoroughly, and expect to outgrow it. What replaces it is direct recognition, where the interval simply has a name the way a colour does, and functional hearing, where you identify notes by their role in a key rather than by measuring distances at all.

sections.heading: Functional Hearing: The Route Past the Plateau
sections.body:
Most people who train intervals in isolation eventually notice something disconcerting: they can name intervals reliably on a drill app and still cannot work out a melody by ear. The reason is that real music is not a sequence of isolated intervals. It happens inside a key, and the ear is strongly, automatically sensitive to key.

Functional hearing, sometimes called tonal or scale-degree hearing, means identifying a note by its role relative to a tonal centre rather than its distance from the previous note. In a key of C, you hear a note as the tonic, the leading note, the dominant, the third degree, and so on. Each degree has a distinct character within the key: the tonic feels settled, the leading note strains upward, the dominant is stable but unfinished, the flattened seventh feels bluesy and pulls downward. These characters are far stronger cues than interval size, and they are why an experienced musician can hear a melody and write it down without consciously measuring a single distance.

The traditional training system for this is solfège using moveable do, in which the tonic is always called do regardless of the actual key, and the degrees run do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, ti. Chromatic degrees have their own syllables. The competing system, fixed do, ties syllables permanently to letter names and is standard in France, Italy and much of Latin America; it trains something closer to absolute pitch and does not develop functional hearing in the same way. For a self-taught adult wanting to play by ear, moveable do or the equivalent numeric system, calling degrees one through seven, is the more useful choice. Which is superior overall is a genuinely long-running pedagogical argument with reasonable people on both sides.

The practical superiority of functional hearing shows up in three places. It is fast, because it requires no computation. It is robust, because a degree keeps its identity even when the melody leaps around. And it self-corrects, because if you misidentify one note the key context immediately makes the next note sound wrong.

Interval training and functional training are not rivals; they solve different problems. Intervals are essential for atonal or highly chromatic music, for identifying chord structures, for tuning, and for any situation where there is no clear key. Functional hearing handles the vast majority of tonal melody and harmony. A complete ear uses both and switches between them without noticing.

The practical implication for a learner is to start interval drills and functional drills at the same time rather than sequentially, and above all to spend the majority of practice time on real music rather than on isolated pairs of notes. The single most common failure in ear training is drilling in a vacuum and never testing the skill against a recording.

sections.heading: A Practical Training Regime
