The default stem length is 3.5 staff spaces, which is one octave, and it lengthens for notes far outside the staff so that the stem reaches at least the middle line. Where beaming forces compression it may shorten, but 2.5 spaces is the usual floor. Beams do far more than replace flags. They are the principal visual signal of metre, and incorrect beaming makes music genuinely hard to read even when every pitch and duration is right. The governing principle is that beam groups should show the beats. In four four, eighth notes are beamed in twos or fours so that beat boundaries stay visible, and a group must not straddle the middle of the bar in a way that hides beat three. In six eight, eighths are beamed in threes because the metre has two dotted quarter beats, and beaming them in twos, which is what naive software does when told the time signature carelessly, converts the music into an unreadable three four. Composers deliberately break these rules to notate syncopation, and that is exactly why the default must be correct: a deviation only reads as deliberate against a reliable norm. The geometry is tightly constrained. A beam is half a staff space thick, and successive beams sit a quarter space apart, giving three quarters of a space from one beam's top edge to the next. Every note in a beamed group shares one stem direction, determined by whichever note lies furthest from the middle line. The beam's slope is not simply drawn between the first and last stems: it is quantised to a small set of permitted slants, traditionally a rise of zero, a quarter, a half, one, one and a half, or two spaces across the group, and it never exceeds roughly two spaces however wide the pitch interval. If the first and last notes are the same pitch the beam is horizontal, even when the inner notes climb. One further rule catches out almost every automatic implementation and is worth knowing by sight. Where a beam falls inside the staff it must sit squarely on a staff line, straddle one, or hang beneath one. What it must not do is stop a sliver short, leaving a white wedge a fraction of a space wide between beam and line, because at reading distance that sliver reads as dirt. Secondary beams for sixteenths and shorter follow the primary, and where a group contains mixed durations the partial or broken beam stub points inward, toward the beat that the note belongs to, so the eye can assign it correctly.

sections.heading: Slurs, Ties and the Fitting of Curves
sections.body: Ties and slurs look almost identical on the page and mean entirely different things, which is why every competent program stores them as distinct objects and why entering one where the other belongs is among the most common errors in amateur scores. A tie joins two notes of the same pitch into one sustained sound; it is a rhythmic device that exists because notation cannot always write a duration directly, as when a note must continue across a barline. A slur joins notes of different pitch and instructs the performer how to play them, meaning legato for most instruments, one bow for strings, one breath for winds and one syllable for singers. Playback engines treat them differently, part extraction treats them differently, and a tie between two different pitches is simply an error. The drawing rules for ties are strict. A tie begins just clear of the right edge of the first notehead and ends just clear of the left edge of the second, curving away from the stem so that it never crosses one. In a chord, ties on the upper notes arch upward and those on the lower notes arch downward, with the middle notes assigned by proximity. The curve itself is not a uniform stroke: it is thickest at the apex, around a fifth of a staff space, and tapers to points at both ends, which is why programs render it as a closed shape bounded by two cubic Bézier curves rather than as a stroked line. When a tie crosses a system break it is cut in two, with the first half curving out from the note and the second half arriving at the note on the new system. Slurs are harder because their endpoints are not fixed by a single note. The side is chosen first: when every stem in the span points the same way, the slur goes on the notehead side, opposite the stems; when stems are mixed, it goes above. The endpoints then attach at a notehead corner or a stem tip, and the two interior control points are set to give a height that grows with the span but is deliberately capped, because a long slur allowed to scale freely balloons halfway up the page. What follows is an iterative fit. The program tests the provisional curve against everything it passes over, including noteheads, accidentals, articulations, ledger lines and other slurs, and if anything intrudes it raises the endpoints, flattens the arch or shifts the control points and tests again, typically over several rounds. That iteration is why slurs are the markings most often needing manual attention. Where the underlying contour is awkward, particularly a slur spanning a large leap or one crossing between staves in piano music, the automatic result can be technically collision free and still ugly. The remedy is to drag the endpoints and control points by hand, but only after the rest of the layout is final, since any reflow will discard the effort.

sections.heading: Collision Avoidance and the Vertical Order of Markings
sections.body: Because vertical position on a staff already means pitch, it cannot be used to keep symbols apart. Everything that is not a notehead therefore has to be arranged outward from the staff in a fixed priority order, and that order is one of the most stable conventions in engraving. Working away from the notes: articulations such as staccato dots, accents and tenuto lines sit closest, effectively touching the note; then ornaments, trills and fingerings; then slurs and phrase marks; then dynamics and hairpins; then expressive words such as dolce or sul ponticello; and finally, at the top of the system, tempo indications and rehearsal marks. Each layer must clear the one beneath it along its whole length, which is why adding a single low note can push a hairpin down and the words beneath it down again. Which side of the staff a marking defaults to depends on the instrument, and the reason is always that something else has already claimed the other side. For most instruments dynamics sit below the staff. In vocal music they move above, because the space below belongs to the lyrics. In keyboard music written on a grand staff, dynamics sit in the gap between the two staves and govern both hands at once, so putting them under the lower staff is an error that quietly changes the meaning. Articulations go on the notehead side, opposite the stem, and a staccato dot inside the staff is placed in a space rather than on a line, where it would be nearly invisible. Within a chord the problems are horizontal as well. Two notes a second apart cannot both sit on the same side of the stem, so one is displaced across it: with the stem up, the lower note keeps its place and the upper moves to the right. Accidentals in a dense chord must be stacked into columns, conventionally placed from the outside inward, each tucked into whatever vertical gap the already placed accidentals leave, and the resulting patterns for common chords are effectively memorised shapes in traditional practice. Modern software solves the general problem with an outline or skyline representation. Rather than treating each object as a rectangle, which is far too crude when a slur must nestle under a rising line of notes, the program builds a piecewise height profile of everything currently occupying the space above or below the staff, then places each new object against that profile and updates it. Overlaps are resolved by pushing outward in priority order and re-running, since moving one object can create a new conflict for another. This works well, and the residual failure rate in practice is small but never zero. Expect to adjust something by hand on perhaps one system in twenty in dense music, and expect those adjustments to be lost if you later change the staff size or page dimensions, which is the reason to leave manual polishing until the very end.

sections.heading: Music Fonts, Optical Sizing and the SMuFL Standard
sections.body: For most of the desktop publishing era, music symbols were distributed as ordinary fonts with music shapes mapped onto ordinary keyboard positions. The first widely used one was Sonata, designed by Cleo Huggins and released by Adobe in 1985, which placed a whole note on the letter w, a half note on h and a quarter note on q. Because later fonts copied that arrangement, notably Petrucci for Finale and Opus for Sibelius, files had a rough chance of surviving a font substitution. The scheme's limit was arithmetic: a single byte encoding offers around two hundred usable positions, while real engraving needs thousands of symbols. Publishers coped by shipping families of specialised fonts and mapping them by private convention, so a score moved between programs almost never rendered correctly. Unicode's Musical Symbols block, added at code points from U+1D100 to U+1D1FF in 2001, is often assumed to have fixed this. It did not. It contains roughly two hundred and twenty characters, enough to write about music in running text but nowhere near enough to engrave it, and it carries no engraving metadata at all. The actual solution arrived in 2013 when Daniel Spreadbury, then at Steinberg, published the Standard Music Font Layout, universally called SMuFL, which reached version 1.0 in 2015 and is now maintained by the W3C Music Notation Community Group. SMuFL does two things. It assigns thousands of glyphs, covering notehead families, articulations, ornaments, microtonal accidentals, percussion pictograms, early music symbols and much else, to fixed positions in the Unicode Private Use Area from U+E000 upward, so that any conforming font can substitute for any other. Separately, and more importantly for layout, each font ships a JSON metadata file carrying engraving defaults such as stem and beam thickness and, per glyph, named anchor points and bounding boxes. A notehead declares exactly where an upward stem should meet its north east corner, which means the host program no longer has to hard code that knowledge for one font. Bravura is the reference implementation, released free under the SIL Open Font License, with Petaluma as its handwritten sibling; Leland, November, Sebastian and the microtonal Ekmelos are among the alternatives. One refinement separates good music fonts from merely competent ones. Glyphs should not simply scale linearly with staff size. A staff line thinned proportionally for a small conductor's score becomes too fine to survive printing, and small noteheads scaled down look anaemic. Well made families therefore apply optical sizing, thickening strokes relatively as the size drops, exactly as text type designers have always done. LilyPond's Emmentaler, descended from the earlier Feta face, is built parametrically in METAFONT precisely so that its glyphs are redrawn rather than merely shrunk at each size. When you set a full score at rastral 7 and the result looks weak and grey, insufficient optical compensation is frequently the reason, and switching font family can help more than adjusting any layout setting.

sections.heading: The Major Programs and How They Differ
sections.body: Four applications dominate serious use, and their differences are architectural rather than cosmetic. Finale, released in 1988 by Coda Music Technology and written initially by Phil Farrand, was the most capable program of its era and remained the standard in North American publishing for decades. Its design philosophy was to expose every coordinate to the user, which made it able to produce literally any notation at the cost of a famously punishing learning curve. In August 2024 its owner MakeMusic announced that development and sales had ended and offered users a crossgrade to Dorico, with support wound down over the following year. Anyone still holding an archive of Finale files should treat exporting them as urgent: while the software still runs, export everything to MusicXML alongside the native files, because a format with no maintainer is a slow data loss event. Sibelius, written by the twin brothers Ben and Jonathan Finn and first released in 1993 for the Acorn Archimedes before reaching Windows and Mac in 1998, took the opposite approach. It made sensible decisions automatically and offered exceptionally fast keyboard driven note entry, which made it the favourite of composers and educators. Avid acquired it in 2006 and closed its London development office in 2012; much of that team moved to Steinberg and built Dorico, first released in October 2016. Dorico's distinguishing feature is the strictness of its separation between musical content and layout, expressed as distinct working modes, which is why a single Dorico project generates full score, condensed score and parts as different views of one dataset rather than as linked copies. MuseScore is free and open source under the GNU General Public License, originating from Werner Schweer's work around 2002 and rebuilt substantially for version 4 in December 2022 with a new engraving engine. By sheer number of users it is now the most widely used notation program in the world, and its output quality is entirely adequate for professional work, which was not true a decade ago. LilyPond, begun in 1996 by Han-Wen Nienhuys and Jan Nieuwenhuizen and part of the GNU project, is a text compiler rather than an interactive editor and produces output many engravers rate the finest available. Two historical notes are worth carrying. SCORE, written by Leland Smith at Stanford and running under DOS, was used by major publishers into the 2000s and its output remains a benchmark against which people still judge modern programs. And on the web, rendering libraries such as Verovio, which draws from the scholarly MEI format, and VexFlow, which underlies several browser applications, have made decent engraving possible inside a web page, which is why online sheet music finally stopped looking like scanned photocopies.

sections.heading: Text-Based Engraving and the Question of Input Method
sections.body: The dominant way to enter music is graphically, but a significant minority of engravers write music as source code and compile it. The case for doing so is not aesthetic stubbornness. A plain text file diffs and merges in version control, so a collaborator's changes can be reviewed line by line and an edition's history is auditable, which matters enormously for critical editions. It is scriptable, so transposing forty parts or applying a house style across a catalogue is a program rather than an afternoon. And it separates content from presentation in the way that a stylesheet does, so the same music can be reissued at a different size or in a different house style without re-editing the music itself. LilyPond is the mature example. Music is written as pitch names with numeric durations, so that the characters c4 d e f produce four quarter notes, a following number changes the duration and a dot after it adds half again. Commands are marked with a leading backslash, structural blocks are delimited by braces, and the whole language is extensible in Scheme through the embedded Guile interpreter, which means genuinely arbitrary notation can be programmed rather than drawn. The workflow is edit, compile, inspect the resulting PDF, repeat, which trades immediate feedback for perfect reproducibility. The editor Frescobaldi softens this considerably by letting you click a note in the preview to jump to the line of source that created it. ABC notation solves a different problem. Devised by Chris Walshaw in the early 1990s for folk and traditional repertoire, it encodes a monophonic tune compactly enough to paste into an email or a forum post. A short header carries the tune index, title, metre, default note length and key, and the melody follows as letters, with case distinguishing octaves. Tens of thousands of traditional tunes circulate in this form, and it remains the standard interchange for that repertoire. For scholarship, the Humdrum kern format serves computational analysis rather than printing. Whatever the format, input speed is dominated by method rather than by software. Mouse entry, in which you pick a duration then click a position, is by a wide margin the slowest and is what most beginners use. Computer keyboard step entry, typing pitch letters and duration numbers, is what professional copyists actually use and is several times faster once learned. A MIDI keyboard used for step entry, supplying pitch with the hands while the computer keyboard supplies rhythm, is comparably fast and less tiring. Real time MIDI recording feels fastest and usually is not, because quantising a human performance into correct notation produces rhythmic debris that takes longer to clean than careful entry would have taken in the first place.

sections.heading: File Formats, Interchange and Long-Term Preservation
sections.body: Three families of format circulate, and confusing them causes most of the frustration people experience moving music between programs. The first is MIDI, standardised in 1983 with the Standard MIDI File following in 1988. MIDI encodes a performance: which key went down, when, how hard, on which channel. It records nothing about how that performance should be written. It cannot distinguish C sharp from D flat, cannot say whether two notes are joined by a tie or a slur, has no concept of voices, beaming, stem direction, articulation as distinct from accent velocity, or any text at all. Importing a MIDI file into a notation program therefore produces a rhythmically approximate mess that must be rebuilt by hand. MIDI is an excellent way to move sound between programs and a bad way to move notation. The second family is notation interchange, dominated by MusicXML. Michael Good developed it at his company Recordare and released version 1.0 in January 2004, explicitly to let scores pass between rival programs. It is XML, and it comes in two arrangements, partwise with each part containing its measures and timewise with each measure containing its parts, mechanically convertible between the two. MakeMusic acquired it in 2011, and stewardship passed to the W3C Music Notation Community Group, which published version 3.1 in 2017 and 4.0 in 2021. The compressed variant, with the extension mxl, is simply a ZIP archive containing the XML plus a small container manifest. Essentially every program reads and writes it, but it is lossy in practice: notation transfers well, while page layout, manual adjustments, custom symbols and playback configuration survive unreliably. Treat a MusicXML export as a faithful copy of the music and an approximation of the page. The third family is scholarly encoding, principally the Music Encoding Initiative. Begun in 1999 by Perry Roland at the University of Virginia and modelled on the Text Encoding Initiative used for literary texts, MEI is built for things printing formats ignore: variant readings between sources, editorial emendations distinguished from what the composer wrote, description of the physical source, links to facsimile images, and older systems such as mensural and neume notation. It is the format of digital musicology rather than of everyday score preparation. For preservation the practical rule is to keep three things for every finished project: the native file in whatever program made it, a MusicXML export, and a PDF. Plain text and XML remain readable for decades; proprietary binary formats depend entirely on a company continuing to exist, a risk that turned concrete for a great many people when Finale was discontinued in 2024. Native extensions worth recognising include musx and the older mus for Finale, sib for Sibelius, dorico, and mscz for MuseScore, the last of which is a ZIP container wrapping readable XML and is therefore a good deal more recoverable than the rest. A successor interchange format called MNX has been under development at the W3C for several years with the aim of fixing MusicXML's structural compromises, but adoption so far is limited and it would be unwise to depend on it today.

sections.heading: Optical Music Recognition and Digitising Printed Scores
sections.body: Optical music recognition is the conversion of an image of a score into editable symbolic music, and it is substantially harder than optical character recognition of text. The difficulty is structural rather than incidental. In text, characters are separated by white space; in music, the staff lines run through and connect every symbol on the system, so the first processing stage must detect and remove five long horizontal lines while preserving the parts of noteheads, stems and slurs that overlap them. Removal inevitably damages symbols, and every later stage inherits that damage. A classical recognition pipeline proceeds in stages. The image is binarised into black and white and deskewed. Staff lines are located, usually by horizontal projection profiles, and removed. The remaining ink is segmented into candidate symbols, which are classified as noteheads, stems, flags, rests, clefs, accidentals and so on. Then comes the genuinely musical stage, in which the system reconstructs meaning: vertical position plus the prevailing clef and key gives pitch, beams and flags give duration, proximity assigns accidentals to noteheads, and a validation pass checks whether the durations in each bar actually add up to the time signature, flagging bars that do not. More recent systems replace much of this with end to end neural sequence models trained on synthetic and annotated scores, which handle noisy input better but fail in less predictable ways. Available tools include PhotoScore from Neuratron, long bundled with Sibelius, SmartScore from Musitek, the open source Audiveris, and several phone applications that scan and play back. Judge their accuracy carefully, because vendors quote per symbol figures that sound better than they are. A typical page of piano music contains well over a thousand symbols, so ninety eight per cent accuracy means roughly twenty errors per page, every one of which must be found by comparing against the original. Clean modern engraving of single line instrumental parts recognises well. Dense orchestral scores, nineteenth century prints with show-through from the reverse side, and handwritten manuscript recognise poorly, and reliable recognition of handwriting remains an open research problem. The honest decision rule is a comparison of times. If proofreading the recognised output will take longer than entering the music from scratch, which is usually the case for anything complex, scanning is a false economy. When you do scan, use a flatbed at 300 to 600 dots per inch in greyscale, keep the page flat and square, and photograph only as a last resort. If you must use a camera, square the lens to the page rather than correcting perspective afterwards, and light the page evenly, since a gradient across the paper defeats binarisation more thoroughly than low resolution does. Note also that recognising a score confers no rights in it; copyright in the music and, in some jurisdictions, a separate shorter right in the publisher's typography, both persist regardless of how the file was made.

sections.heading: Preparing Performance Parts: A Working Procedure
sections.body: Extracting parts is where an otherwise good score becomes usable or useless, and it is the stage amateurs most often skip. A part is not a slice of the score. It is a separate document with different requirements: a much larger staff size because it is read at distance, a completely independent casting off because the player only needs their own line, multi-bar rests collapsing empty stretches into a single numbered bar, cues so the player knows what to listen for before an entry, and page turns that fall where a hand is free. Every modern program generates parts that stay linked to the score, so a correction made in either propagates, which is the single most valuable feature in the category; the older practice of copying music into fresh documents guaranteed that score and parts would diverge. Work through the following sequence once the music itself is finalised, and resist the temptation to polish anything by hand until the end, because reflowing the layout discards manual adjustments.
steps: Fix the physical page and staff size before anything else, choosing from the reading conditions: around 7 mm staff height for parts read at two metres, smaller only for scores read close up on a lit podium.

Confirm each instrument's transposition and clef are set as instrument properties, never by writing transposed notes into a concert-pitch staff, and verify by toggling the concert pitch view and checking the sounding result.
Generate parts from the score using the program's linked-part mechanism rather than copying music into new documents, so that later corrections propagate in both directions automatically.

Switch on multi-bar rests in the parts, then force breaks in them at rehearsal marks, tempo changes, metre changes and key changes, since a rest bar that spans a tempo change hides that change from the player.

Add cues before every entry that follows more than about eight bars of rest: small noteheads, the cued instrument named, transposed for the reading player rather than the sounding player, and placed so the player's own entry is unmistakable.

Re-cast off each part independently of the score, aiming for four to six bars per system in busy music and more in sparse music, then check that no system is visibly darker or paler than its neighbours.

Walk every page turn by miming the part in real time, and where a turn lands with no free bars, fix it physically with a fold-out page, an even page count that lies flat, a duplicated page, or staggered turns between desk partners.
Proofread the part against the score bar by bar, ideally with a second person reading one aloud, checking accidentals, ties across barlines, dynamics and rehearsal mark numbering.
Print one copy at final size, put it on a stand, and read it at playing distance in the lighting the players will actually have before you export anything.
Export to PDF with all fonts embedded, at the exact final page dimensions, and archive the native file, a MusicXML export and the PDF together.

sections.heading: Failure Modes, Limits and Repairs
sections.body: A predictable set of failures accounts for most unusable scores, and nearly all of them are diagnosable by symptom. Nonsensical accidental spellings, with E sharp where F belongs and double flats appearing from nowhere, almost always mean the music arrived as MIDI, which carries no spelling information; the repair is to respell systematically rather than note by note, and the lesson is not to use MIDI as an interchange format. Beaming that groups eighth notes in twos throughout a compound metre means the time signature was set without telling the program the beat grouping, and fixing the time signature properly usually corrects every bar at once. Symbols that appear as empty rectangles or wrong characters when someone else opens your PDF mean the music font was not embedded at export. Always embed, and check by opening the PDF on a machine that does not have the font installed. Music that is clipped at the edges when printed in another country is almost always an A4 against US Letter mismatch, the two being different in both dimensions; set the page size to the destination's paper rather than relying on shrink to fit, which silently reduces your carefully chosen staff size. The most demoralising failure is losing an afternoon of manual adjustment because a later change to page size, staff size or a single bar caused everything to reflow. This is not a bug and cannot be engineered away, since the adjustments were expressed relative to a layout that no longer exists. The discipline that prevents it is strict ordering: finish the notes, then the dynamics and articulations, then the page and staff dimensions, then the casting off, and only then touch a single slur by hand. If a file becomes genuinely corrupt or accumulates inexplicable layout behaviour, exporting to MusicXML and importing into a fresh document strips the accumulated state, at the cost of losing formatting you will have to redo. Several smaller faults recur. Missing courtesy accidentals, the reminders placed in parentheses when a note returns after an accidental in the previous bar, cause more wrong notes in rehearsal than any other omission. And editing by ear from the program's playback rather than by eye from the page produces scores that sound right and read badly, because playback ignores the visual conventions that matter. Two limits are worth stating plainly. First, no program understands music. Every automatic decision is a heuristic tuned to common repertoire, and unusual notation, contemporary techniques, early music and anything genuinely novel will need manual work no matter which application you buy. Second, and more important, no amount of screen inspection substitutes for the only real test. Give the part to a competent player who has never seen it and ask them to sight-read it once, then watch where they hesitate. Every hesitation marks a place where the notation failed, and that feedback is worth more than any checklist, including this one.

guides.title: Pitch, Frequency and the Harmonic Series
guides.summary: What pitch is physically and perceptually, how vibrating strings and air columns generate the harmonic series, and how that series produces timbre, consonance, scales, the tuning problem and the compromises of temperament.

sections.heading: What Pitch Is and Why It Matters
sections.body: Pitch is the quality of a sound that lets us arrange notes from low to high, and it is the single organising dimension of nearly all the world's music. Melody is a shape drawn in pitch. Harmony is several pitches at once. A scale is a chosen subset of the available pitches. Tuning is the argument about exactly where those pitches should sit. Almost everything a musician learns about theory turns out, on inspection, to be a consequence of a handful of physical facts about how objects vibrate, and the purpose of studying pitch properly is to see those consequences rather than memorising the rules they generate. The physical basis is straightforward. A sounding object vibrates, alternately pushing and pulling on the air next to it. That produces travelling regions of slightly raised and slightly lowered air pressure, which spread outward at the speed of sound and eventually reach an eardrum, pushing it in and out. Ordinary conversation involves pressure fluctuations of about 0.02 pascals against a background atmospheric pressure of roughly 101,000 pascals, a variation of about two parts in ten million, and the quietest sound a healthy young person can detect is around 20 micropascals, a displacement of the eardrum smaller than the diameter of a hydrogen atom. If those pressure fluctuations repeat in a regular cycle, we hear a pitch. If they do not repeat, we hear noise: a cymbal crash, a hiss, a handclap. The distinction between a note and a noise is essentially the distinction between periodic and aperiodic vibration. Two things follow that are worth stating at the outset because they are constantly confused. The first is that pitch is a perception and frequency is a physical measurement, and although they correspond closely they are not the same thing; the ear does substantial interpretive work between one and the other. The second is that almost no musical sound consists of a single frequency. A plucked string, a bowed string, a blown pipe and a sung vowel all vibrate simultaneously at a whole family of related frequencies, and it is the pattern and relative strength of that family that gives each instrument its recognisable voice. That family is the harmonic series, and it is the central object of this subject. Understanding it explains why a trumpet and a clarinet sound different, why some pairs of notes sound sweet and others harsh, why keyboards have to be tuned slightly wrong on purpose, why a bugle can only play certain notes, and why a gamelan orchestra sounds unlike anything in Western music. It also explains a great deal about the human voice, about hearing loss, about audio engineering and about why a compressed music file can throw away most of its data without you noticing.

sections.heading: Frequency, Period, Wavelength and the Units
sections.body: Frequency is the number of complete vibration cycles occurring each second, and it is measured in hertz, abbreviated Hz, after the German physicist Heinrich Hertz who between 1886 and 1889 produced and detected the electromagnetic waves that James Clerk Maxwell had predicted. The unit was adopted by the International Electrotechnical Commission in 1930 and gradually replaced the older and more self-explanatory cycles per second over the following decades. One hertz is one cycle per second, so a string vibrating back and forth 440 times each second has a frequency of 440 Hz. The period is the reciprocal: the time taken for a single cycle. At 440 Hz the period is 1 divided by 440, about 2.27 milliseconds. Wavelength is the physical distance the disturbance travels during one period, equal to the speed of sound divided by the frequency. The speed of sound in air is not fixed but depends mainly on temperature, following approximately 331.3 plus 0.606 times the temperature in degrees Celsius, in metres per second; at 20 degrees Celsius that gives about 343 metres per second. A 440 Hz note therefore has a wavelength of roughly 0.78 metres, while a low organ pedal note at 32.7 Hz has a wavelength of over ten metres, which is why the pipes producing it are so long. The healthy young human ear responds to frequencies between roughly 20 Hz and 20,000 Hz, though the upper limit falls steadily with age in a process called presbycusis, so that many people over sixty hear little above 12,000 Hz and many over seventy little above 8,000 Hz. Musical pitch occupies the lower and middle part of that range: the lowest note on a standard piano, A0, is about 27.5 Hz, and the highest, C8, about 4,186 Hz. Everything above that is harmonics and brilliance rather than melody. The reference point for the whole modern system is the note A above middle C, called A4, standardised at 440 Hz by international agreement, formalised as ISO 16. That standard is recent and the value is arbitrary. Surviving organs and tuning forks show European pitch varying from roughly 392 Hz to 465 Hz for the same written note between the seventeenth and nineteenth centuries, which is why period-instrument ensembles commonly tune to 415 Hz for Baroque music, almost exactly a semitone below modern pitch, and why some orchestras today tune sharp at 442 or 443 Hz for a brighter sound. One further convention is worth fixing early. Because frequency doubles at every octave, note names in the scientific pitch notation used here carry an octave number that increments at each C: A4 is 440 Hz, A5 is 880, A3 is 220, A2 is 110 and A0 is 27.5. Every octave up doubles the number of hertz, which means that the top octave of a piano occupies more than 2,000 Hz of the spectrum while the bottom octave occupies less than 28. That asymmetry has real consequences: bass notes are crowded together in frequency and take many milliseconds to establish, which is why low pitches are harder to tune and harder to localise.

sections.heading: From Air Pressure to Perceived Pitch: How the Ear Works
sections.body: The ear converts a pressure wave into a frequency analysis, and it does so mechanically before any nerve is involved. Sound funnels down the ear canal and vibrates the eardrum, a membrane about 8 to 10 millimetres across. Three tiny bones in the middle ear — the malleus, incus and stapes, the smallest bones in the body — transmit that motion to the oval window of the cochlea. Their job is impedance matching: air is thin and easily moved, the fluid inside the cochlea is not, and without a mechanical transformer almost all the sound energy would simply reflect off the fluid surface. The lever action of the bones combined with the roughly twentyfold area difference between eardrum and oval window produces a pressure gain of about 20 to 30 times, recovering most of what would otherwise be lost. The cochlea itself is a fluid-filled tube of about 35 millimetres coiled into two and a half turns like a snail shell. Running along its length is the basilar membrane, and the crucial fact about this membrane is that its mechanical properties change continuously from one end to the other: near the oval window, the basal end, it is narrow and stiff, while at the far apical end it is wider and floppier. A travelling wave set up in the cochlear fluid therefore peaks at a different position depending on frequency — high frequencies near the base, low frequencies near the apex. This spatial mapping is called tonotopy, and it means the cochlea performs something very like a mechanical frequency analysis, splitting a complex sound into its components and assigning each to a place. Hermann von Helmholtz proposed the essentials of this place theory in the 1860s; Georg von Békésy demonstrated the travelling wave directly and received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1961 for it. Sitting on the basilar membrane, the organ of Corti carries about 3,500 inner hair cells in a single row, which do the actual transduction, and roughly 12,000 outer hair cells in three rows, which act as an active amplifier, physically changing length in time with the sound to sharpen the tuning and boost quiet sounds by up to a thousandfold. Damage to the outer hair cells from noise exposure or ageing causes both loss of sensitivity and loss of frequency selectivity, which is why hearing loss so often shows up as difficulty following speech in a noisy room rather than as simple quietness. Place is not the whole story. Auditory nerve fibres also fire in step with the waveform, a phenomenon called phase locking, reliably up to about 4,000 or 5,000 hertz, which provides a second, timing-based code for pitch. Most researchers now regard pitch perception as using both.

sections.heading: Pitch Is Not Simply Frequency
sections.body: For a simple sine tone, pitch tracks frequency closely, but the relationship is neither linear nor exact, and several well-documented departures matter musically. The first is that the mapping is logarithmic rather than proportional. Doubling a frequency always produces the same perceptual jump, the octave, whether you go from 100 to 200 Hz or 4,000 to 8,000 Hz, even though the second jump involves forty times as many hertz. Musical intervals are ratios, not differences, and every convenient unit for measuring them — the octave, the semitone, the cent — is logarithmic for this reason. The second departure is octave equivalence: notes an octave apart sound so alike that nearly every musical culture gives them the same name, which is why pitch is often modelled as a helix, combining a continuous height dimension with a circular chroma dimension that repeats each octave. The third and most striking is the phenomenon of the missing fundamental. Play a complex tone containing components at 400, 600, 800 and 1,000 Hz but nothing at 200 Hz, and listeners hear a pitch of 200 Hz anyway, because that is the frequency of which all present components are multiples. The brain infers the fundamental from the pattern of its harmonics. This is not a laboratory curiosity: a telephone line historically passed only about 300 to 3,400 Hz, cutting off the fundamental of every adult male voice, and small loudspeakers and phone speakers reproduce almost nothing below 150 Hz, yet bass lines and low voices remain audible and correctly pitched through both. The effect was systematically described by the Dutch scientist Jan Schouten in 1938 and is variously called residue pitch, virtual pitch or periodicity pitch. There are smaller effects too. The perceived pitch of a pure tone shifts slightly with loudness, low tones sounding flatter and high tones sharper as level rises, an effect of a few percent at extreme levels and negligible at normal ones. Very short sounds have no definite pitch at all, because the ear needs several cycles to establish periodicity: below about 10 milliseconds a tone is heard as a click. The smallest pitch change a person can detect, the just-noticeable difference, is roughly 0.2 to 0.5 percent in the mid range for a trained listener, which is about 3 to 8 cents, or somewhere between a twentieth and a sixth of a semitone. And the pitch of complex sounds can be genuinely ambiguous: bells, gongs and some synthesised tones support more than one reasonable pitch judgement, and different listeners will confidently disagree. The missing-fundamental effect also founds a branch of audio engineering. Psychoacoustic bass enhancement circuits in phones, laptops and small speakers deliberately synthesise the harmonics of a bass note that the driver cannot physically reproduce, letting the listener's own auditory system supply the fundamental that was never radiated. The same logic underlies perceptual audio compression: formats such as MP3 and AAC discard components that the ear cannot resolve because louder neighbouring components mask them, achieving compression ratios around ten to one with little audible loss. Both technologies work because hearing is an act of inference, not a measurement.

sections.heading: The Vibrating String: Modes and Mersenne's Laws
sections.body: A string stretched between two fixed points is the clearest illustration of how the harmonic series arises, and the reason is a boundary condition: the string cannot move at either end. Any vibration must therefore be a standing wave with a node, a point of no motion, at each end. Only certain wavelengths satisfy that requirement. The simplest is a single arch with the whole string swinging as one, which fits exactly half a wavelength into the string length, giving a wavelength of twice the length. The next possibility divides the string in two, each half moving opposite to the other with a stationary node at the centre, and fits one whole wavelength. The next fits one and a half, and so on indefinitely. In general the permitted wavelengths are 2L divided by n, where L is the string length and n is any positive whole number. Since frequency is wave speed divided by wavelength, the permitted frequencies are n times v divided by 2L. That is the entire origin of the harmonic series: the possible frequencies are whole-number multiples of the lowest one, purely because whole numbers of half-wavelengths are the only shapes that fit between two fixed ends. A real string does not choose one mode. Pluck it, bow it or strike it and it vibrates in many modes at once, their relative strengths determined by where and how it was excited. Pluck at the midpoint and you strongly excite modes with an antinode there, meaning the odd-numbered ones, while suppressing the even ones which have a node at the centre; pluck near the bridge and you excite many high modes, producing a bright, thin sound. Guitarists and harpsichord builders exploit this constantly, and it is why the same string sounds mellow near the fingerboard and nasal near the bridge. The wave speed itself is set by the string's physical properties: it equals the square root of tension divided by mass per unit length. Combining that with the frequency formula gives the three relationships published by the French friar Marin Mersenne in his Harmonie universelle of 1636 and still known as Mersenne's laws. Frequency is inversely proportional to length, so halving the length doubles the pitch, which is why a fret halfway along a guitar string gives the octave. Frequency is proportional to the square root of tension, so to raise a string a whole tone, a ratio of about 1.122, you must increase tension by about 26 percent. And frequency is inversely proportional to the square root of mass per unit length, which is why bass strings are thick or wound with wire rather than absurdly long or slack.

sections.heading: Air Columns: Open Pipes, Stopped Pipes and Why the Clarinet Is Odd
sections.body: Wind instruments work by the same standing-wave logic, but their boundary conditions differ and this produces one of the most useful facts in orchestration. In a tube the vibrating quantity is air pressure and air motion. At an open end the air is free to move and pressure stays near atmospheric, so an open end forces a pressure node and a displacement antinode. At a closed end the air cannot move, so a closed end forces the opposite. A tube open at both ends therefore needs a pressure node at each end, which is mathematically the same condition as a string fixed at both ends: permitted wavelengths are 2L over n, permitted frequencies are n times v over 2L, and the complete harmonic series is available. A flute, a recorder and an open organ flue pipe behave this way, which is why they overblow at the octave: blow harder and the pipe jumps to its second mode at twice the frequency. A tube closed at one end and open at the other must have a node at one end and an antinode at the other, and the shortest shape satisfying that is a quarter of a wavelength rather than a half. The permitted wavelengths become 4L over odd numbers only, and the frequencies are the odd harmonics: the fundamental, then three times it, then five times, and so on. Two consequences follow. A stopped pipe sounds an octave lower than an open pipe of the same length, which is why organ builders use stopped ranks to obtain deep notes from short pipes and save enormous amounts of space and metal. And a stopped pipe overblows not at the octave but at the twelfth, a ratio of three to one. The clarinet is acoustically a stopped cylindrical pipe, closed at the mouthpiece by the reed, and this is exactly why it overblows at the twelfth rather than the octave, why its lower register sounds hollow and woody with its weak even harmonics, and why it needs more keys than a flute to fill the larger gap between registers. Conical instruments break the pattern in an instructive way. The oboe, bassoon and saxophone are all reed instruments closed at the mouthpiece, yet a complete cone behaves acoustically like an open pipe, supporting the full harmonic series and overblowing at the octave. That is why a saxophone sounds nothing like a clarinet despite using a nearly identical mouthpiece and reed. Real pipes also need an end correction, because the air just outside an open end participates in the motion; the effective length is longer than the physical one by roughly 0.6 times the radius at a flanged open end, a small factor that instrument makers must account for precisely.

sections.heading: The Harmonic Series: The Ladder Itself
sections.body: Take any fundamental frequency and multiply it by 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and so on, and you have the harmonic series. Working from a low C at about 65.4 Hz, the first sixteen harmonics fall at 65.4, 130.8, 196.2, 261.6, 327, 392.4, 457.8, 523.2, 588.6, 654, 719.4, 784.8, 850.2, 915.6, 981 and 1046.4 hertz. Translated into note names, that ladder reads C, C, G, C, E, G, a flattish B flat, C, D, E, a half-sharp F, G, a flat A flat, the same flattish B flat, B, C. Several structural features are worth reading off directly. The intervals between consecutive harmonics shrink steadily as you go up, because the ratio between harmonic n and n plus 1 approaches one. The gap from the first to the second harmonic is 2:1, an octave. From second to third is 3:2, a perfect fifth. From third to fourth is 4:3, a perfect fourth. From fourth to fifth is 5:4, a major third; from fifth to sixth, 6:5, a minor third. Beyond that the steps become smaller than any interval in common Western use. Every power of two — harmonics 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 — is the same note in a higher octave, which is the physical root of octave equivalence. Every consonant interval of Western music appears somewhere in the first six harmonics, and the major triad emerges unbidden as harmonics 4, 5 and 6. That is not a convention; it is a shape sitting inside every sounding string. Three harmonics deserve special mention because they do not fit the twelve-note keyboard at all. The seventh harmonic, at a ratio of 7:4 to the fundamental, is about 31 cents flat of the equal-tempered minor seventh — noticeably flat, roughly a third of a semitone. It is a genuinely sweet, settled sound when it appears in barbershop singing or in brass playing, and it is the reason a well-tuned dominant seventh chord can sound richer in an a cappella group than on a piano. The eleventh harmonic, at 11:8, lands almost exactly midway between a perfect fourth and an augmented fourth, about 551 cents, and is often called the alphorn fa after the Swiss instrument that plays it. The thirteenth is similarly homeless. Composers from Britten to Ligeti have written for natural horn or unstopped brass precisely to get these out-of-tune-sounding notes, and folk traditions that use natural instruments simply accept them as correct. The general word for a component of a complex tone is a partial. When the partials happen to be whole-number multiples of the fundamental, they are called harmonics, and an overtone is any partial above the fundamental — so the second harmonic is the first overtone, a numbering mismatch that causes endless confusion and is best avoided by speaking only of harmonics.

sections.heading: Fourier, Spectrum and the Analysis of a Waveform
sections.body: The mathematical statement underlying everything so far was made by the French mathematician Joseph Fourier, who presented it in 1807 and published it fully in his Théorie analytique de la chaleur in 1822 while studying heat conduction rather than sound. Fourier's theorem asserts that any periodic waveform, however jagged, can be expressed as a sum of pure sine waves at whole-number multiples of the repetition frequency, each with its own amplitude and phase. The claim was controversial at the time — Lagrange among others objected that it could not possibly represent a discontinuous shape — and it required a century of analysis to state its conditions rigorously. Musically its meaning is simple and powerful: a complex periodic sound is nothing more or less than a stack of harmonics with particular strengths. A sawtooth wave contains every harmonic with amplitudes falling as one over n. A square wave contains only the odd harmonics, also falling as one over n, which is why a square wave and a clarinet share a family resemblance. A triangle wave contains odd harmonics falling much faster, as one over n squared, giving a soft flute-like sound. A pure sine wave contains only the first harmonic and sounds characterless, almost like a hearing test. This decomposition is what an instrument's spectrum shows: a plot of amplitude against frequency, with a line at each harmonic whose height gives its strength. Where a waveform plot shows the sound in time, the spectrum shows it in frequency, and the two contain the same information. A spectrogram combines both, plotting frequency against time with intensity as brightness, and it is the standard tool for looking at speech and music. Georg Ohm proposed in 1843 that the ear performs essentially this analysis, hearing the harmonic components rather than the waveform shape, and Helmholtz developed the idea at length in his 1863 book On the Sensations of Tone, which remains the foundation of musical acoustics. One important qualification is that phase — the relative timing of the harmonics — has surprisingly little effect on perceived timbre for steady tones, which is roughly what Ohm's law asserts, though it is not exactly true and phase relationships do matter for some sounds and for spatial hearing. There is a deep trade-off buried in all this, sometimes called the uncertainty principle of signal analysis: the more precisely you localise a sound in time, the less precisely you can determine its frequency, and vice versa. This is why very short notes have vague pitch, why bass notes take longer to identify than treble ones, and why any real spectrum analyser must choose a window length and accept the corresponding blur.

sections.heading: Timbre: Why Two Instruments at the Same Pitch Differ
sections.body: Play A440 on a violin, a flute, an oboe and a piano and every one produces a fundamental at 440 Hz with harmonics at 880, 1320, 1760 and so on. The frequencies are identical. What differs is the recipe: how strong each harmonic is, how those strengths change as the note evolves, and what happens in the first few hundredths of a second. That combination is timbre, sometimes called tone colour, and it is the reason you can identify a friend's voice in one syllable. The steady-state spectrum does much of the work. A flute is dominated by its fundamental with weak upper harmonics, giving a pure, hollow sound. A violin has strong energy through the first ten or more harmonics, giving richness and carrying power. An oboe emphasises harmonics around 1,000 to 1,500 Hz, producing its nasal focus. A clarinet in its low register has weak even harmonics, following from its stopped cylindrical bore, giving a hollow woody quality. Some instruments and all voices have formants: fixed resonances of the body or the vocal tract that reinforce whatever harmonics happen to fall within them, regardless of the note being played. Vowels in speech are essentially formant patterns, with the distinction between the vowels in heed, head and hod carried by the first two formants, and a trained operatic singer develops the singer's formant, a cluster of energy near 2,800 to 3,000 Hz that lets a voice carry over an orchestra, which has relatively little energy there. But the steady state is only part of the story, and often not the most important part. The attack transient — the first 20 to 100 milliseconds, containing the scrape of the bow catching, the chiff of air across the flute's edge, the thud of hammer on string — carries an enormous share of identification. In classic experiments, recordings with their attacks edited off become remarkably hard to tell apart, and a piano note played backwards sounds like an organ. Equally important is how the spectrum evolves: on nearly every instrument the higher harmonics decay faster than the fundamental, so a note grows mellower as it dies, and playing more loudly usually adds upper harmonics rather than simply increasing volume, which is why a fortissimo trumpet sounds brassy and sharp-edged rather than just louder. Timbre is therefore multi-dimensional and no single number captures it, though brightness, measured as the spectral centroid or the centre of gravity of the spectrum, correlates with a great deal of what listeners report. Two consequences are worth drawing out. The first is that an instrument's body does not add harmonics so much as filter them: a violin's top plate, back and enclosed air have their own resonances, notably a main air resonance near 275 Hz and a main wood resonance near 460 Hz, which amplify whichever harmonics fall on them. Two violins differ because their filters differ, not their strings. The second is that register matters in orchestration: the same written pitch at the top of a clarinet's range and the bottom of a flute's produces entirely different balances of harmonics, and composers think in these regional colours.

sections.heading: Consonance, Roughness and Critical Bands
sections.body: Why do some pairs of notes sound smooth and others harsh? The Pythagorean answer, over two thousand years old, was that intervals expressible in small whole-number ratios are consonant, and the observation is correct even if the mystical numerology attached to it was not. The modern mechanistic explanation was developed by Helmholtz and refined by the Dutch researchers Reinier Plomp and Willem Levelt in a 1965 study that remains the standard reference. It rests on the concept of the critical band. Because the cochlea maps frequency onto position, two tones close together in frequency excite overlapping regions of the basilar membrane and cannot be resolved separately. The width of that region of interference is the critical band, roughly 100 Hz for tones below about 500 Hz and roughly a fifth to a third of an octave above that. When two tones fall within a critical band but are not identical, they interfere, producing an unpleasant fluctuating sensation called roughness. Plomp and Levelt measured how roughness varies with separation and found that it is zero when the tones coincide, rises to a maximum when they are separated by about a quarter of a critical bandwidth, and falls back to near zero once separation exceeds the critical band. Now apply that to real instruments, which produce not one frequency but a stack of harmonics. When two complex tones sound together, every harmonic of one can interfere with every harmonic of the other. If the fundamentals are in a simple ratio, large numbers of harmonics coincide exactly and produce no roughness at all. For an octave, 2:1, every harmonic of the upper note coincides with an even harmonic of the lower. For a perfect fifth, 3:2, every second harmonic of the upper coincides with every third of the lower. For a major third, 5:4, the coincidences are sparser. For a tritone or a minor second, hardly any harmonics coincide and many land within a critical band of each other, generating substantial roughness. On this account consonance is not a mystical property of numbers but a measurable consequence of harmonic overlap, and the small-integer rule works precisely because small integers produce many coincidences. The theory makes a strong and testable prediction: an instrument whose partials are not harmonic should have a different consonance pattern, and different scales should suit it. That prediction appears to hold, which is a considerable point in the theory's favour. It should be said plainly, though, that roughness explains sensory consonance and not musical consonance. Whether a chord sounds resolved or unstable in a piece of music depends heavily on style, expectation and training; a dominant seventh is acoustically rough yet functions as an ordinary, unremarkable sound to any listener raised on tonal music.

sections.heading: Just Intonation: Scales Built from Small Whole Numbers
sections.body: If consonance comes from simple frequency ratios, the natural way to build a scale is to use those ratios directly. That approach is called just intonation, and a major scale in just intonation on a fundamental of C uses the ratios 1:1 for C, 9:8 for D, 5:4 for E, 4:3 for F, 3:2 for G, 5:3 for A, 15:8 for B and 2:1 for the upper C. Taking C as 264 Hz for arithmetical convenience, those give 264, 297, 330, 352, 396, 440, 495 and 528 Hz. The elegance is in what the ratios do to chords. The tonic triad C-E-G becomes 4:5:6 exactly, the subdominant F-A-C becomes 4:5:6 exactly, and the dominant G-B-D becomes 4:5:6 exactly. All three principal triads are pure, meaning their harmonics coincide precisely and no roughness at all is generated. Unaccompanied choirs, string quartets and barbershop quartets gravitate towards these ratios spontaneously because pure chords ring in a way that tempered ones do not; the sensation of a chord suddenly locking and seeming to grow louder is the sound of harmonics aligning. Just intonation has, however, a fatal structural problem for any instrument with fixed pitches. Notice that the step from C to D is 9:8, and the step from D to E is 10:9. These are different sizes — 204 cents and 182 cents respectively — so there are two different whole tones in the scale, differing by 81:80, a discrepancy of about 21.5 cents known as the syntonic comma. Roughly a fifth of a semitone, it is far too large to ignore. The consequences appear immediately when you try to modulate. The D at 297 Hz is correct as the fifth of G and as the ninth of C, but the D required to make a pure minor triad on the second degree, D-F-A, would need to be 293.3 Hz, a syntonic comma lower. A keyboard cannot have both. Worse, the problem multiplies with every new key: a keyboard tuned justly in C is progressively more out of tune the further you move around the circle of fifths, and by the time you reach a remote key some intervals become genuinely unusable, producing the notoriously howling interval known to organ builders as the wolf fifth. Instruments with flexible pitch — voice, violin family, trombone, fretless bass — can and do adjust in real time, which is why ensembles of them can play in something close to just intonation. Anything with fixed pitches must compromise. A further complication shows the problem is not merely practical. A choir singing a progression that returns to its starting chord through a chain of pure intervals will, if every interval is tuned justly, arrive a syntonic comma below where it began. This is comma drift, and unaccompanied choirs really do sink over long passages for exactly this reason. Good directors manage it by choosing which intervals to temper slightly, usually widening thirds a little rather than letting the tonic slide. Just intonation is therefore best understood not as a rival system to equal temperament but as the acoustic ideal flexible performers approach locally, chord by chord.

sections.heading: Temperament: The Comma Problem and Equal Division
sections.body: The deepest obstacle in tuning is a bare arithmetical fact that no ingenuity can remove. Stack twelve perfect fifths, each a ratio of 3:2, and you might expect to land exactly seven octaves above where you started, since the circle of fifths appears to close after twelve steps. It does not. Twelve fifths give 531,441 divided by 4,096, roughly 129.746; seven octaves give exactly 128. The excess, a ratio of 531,441 to 524,288 or about 23.46 cents, is the Pythagorean comma — nearly a quarter of a semitone, easily audible and quite unacceptable to leave in one place. The reason is that 2 and 3 are different prime numbers, so twelve fifths nearly closing is a numerical coincidence rather than an identity. Every fixed-pitch tuning system in history is a different strategy for disposing of that leftover. Pythagorean tuning, common in medieval Europe, keeps eleven fifths pure and dumps the whole comma into the twelfth, producing one appalling wolf fifth to be avoided, along with very wide major thirds of 408 cents — which is precisely why medieval theory classed thirds as dissonances. Meantone temperament, dominant from roughly 1500 to 1700, does the opposite: quarter-comma meantone narrows each fifth to about 696.6 cents so that major thirds come out pure at 386.3, suiting Renaissance harmony, at the cost of a wolf usually placed between G sharp and E flat and only six to eight usable keys. The well temperaments of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, associated with Andreas Werckmeister, distribute the comma unevenly so every key is playable but each has its own character; this is very likely the world of Bach's Well-Tempered Clavier, whose title advertises playability in all twenty-four keys rather than equal temperament as such; which scheme Bach preferred is unknown and still argued. Equal temperament settles the matter by spreading the error perfectly evenly. Each semitone becomes the twelfth root of two, about 1.0594631, so twelve of them multiply to exactly 2 and the circle truly closes. The mathematics was published independently by the Chinese prince Zhu Zaiyu in 1584 and the Flemish engineer Simon Stevin at almost the same date, though keyboards took until the mid-nineteenth century to adopt it. The unit for auditing the compromise is the cent, introduced by Alexander Ellis in the 1880s: a hundredth of a tempered semitone, 1,200 to the octave, with the size of any ratio r given by 1,200 times the base-two logarithm of r. Being logarithmic, cents add where ratios multiply. The accounting is unforgiving. The just fifth measures 701.955 cents, so the tempered fifth is flat by 1.955 — imperceptible. The just major third measures 386.31, so the tempered third is sharp by 13.69 cents, audible as a persistent slow beating in every sustained major chord on a piano. The just minor third is flat of the tempered one by about 15.6 cents, and the harmonic seventh by 31. In return come unlimited modulation, transposition without retuning, enharmonic equivalence and workable frets — the freedom that made later harmony possible, bought at the price that no interval but the octave is ever exactly in tune again.

sections.heading: Playing the Series: Bugles, Natural Horns, Harmonics and Overtone Singing
sections.body: The harmonic series is not merely a theoretical construct; several instruments play it directly and can play nothing else. A bugle is a length of tubing with a mouthpiece and no valves or holes whatever, so the only notes available are the modes of the tube itself. The player selects among them with lip tension and air speed alone, and in practice the usable range is harmonics 2 through 6, which on a B flat bugle give the notes B flat, F, B flat, D and F. Every traditional bugle call — reveille, taps, the cavalry charge — is built from those five notes, and their characteristic sound, all leaps and fanfares with no stepwise melody in the lower range, is a direct consequence. The natural trumpet and natural horn of the Baroque and Classical eras worked the same way, which is why their parts sit very high, up around harmonics 8 to 16, where the series finally becomes dense enough to permit something like a scale; playing in that register is called the clarino style and demands extraordinary control. Horn players later learned to lower individual harmonics by inserting the hand into the bell, a technique called hand-stopping developed around 1750 and usually credited to Anton Joseph Hampel in Dresden, which gave a full chromatic scale at the cost of a muffled tone on the stopped notes. Valves, invented around 1815, solved the problem completely by switching in extra lengths of tubing to give the player several harmonic series to choose from. String players access the series a different way. Touch a vibrating string lightly at exactly the halfway point and you damp every mode with an antinode there while leaving the second harmonic untouched, so the string sounds an octave higher with a pure, flute-like quality. Touch at a third of the length and you get the third harmonic, a twelfth above; at a quarter, two octaves. These natural harmonics are standard technique on violin, guitar, harp and double bass. The human voice can do it too. In the overtone singing traditions of Tuva and Mongolia, known as khoomei and its several styles, a singer holds a steady low fundamental and reshapes the mouth and tongue to create a sharp movable resonance that picks out individual harmonics, typically the sixth through twelfth, making them audible as a separate whistling melody above the drone. Nothing extra is produced; the harmonics were always there, and the singer is filtering rather than generating. Several other traditions live on the series. The Swiss alphorn, a straight wooden tube three to four metres long with no holes, plays nothing but its natural harmonics, and its eleventh partial — between F and F sharp — is so recognisable that it is named the alphorn fa and was quoted by Brahms. The didgeridoo sounds one drone while the player's mouth sweeps resonances across its harmonics, and the jaw harp works the same way. Trombonists occupy a middle position, choosing a harmonic with the lips then adjusting length continuously with the slide, which is why trombone sections can tune chords justly.

sections.heading: Beats and Practical Tuning by Ear
sections.body: When two tones of nearly the same frequency sound together, they alternately reinforce and cancel, producing a slow rise and fall in loudness called beating. The beat rate equals the difference between the two frequencies, so 440 Hz against 442 Hz beats twice per second. This is the single most useful practical fact in tuning, because it converts a small pitch error into a countable rhythm that even an untrained ear can detect with far greater precision than it can judge pitch directly. A difference of one cent at 440 Hz is a difference of about 0.25 Hz, giving one beat every four seconds, and a careful listener can hear that. Fine tuning is therefore not really a pitch task at all; it is a task of slowing a beat until it stops. As the frequency difference grows past about 15 or 20 hertz the fluctuation becomes too fast to count and is heard instead as roughness, and beyond the critical band the two tones separate cleanly into two distinct pitches. Beats also occur between harmonics rather than fundamentals, which is what makes practical tuning possible on real instruments. To tune a violin's A and E strings a perfect fifth apart, the player listens not to the fundamentals but to the coincidence of the third harmonic of A with the second harmonic of E, both near 1,320 Hz, and adjusts until that beating stops. Piano technicians work entirely this way, using documented beat rates: tuning equal temperament by ear means deliberately setting each fifth to beat at a specific slow rate, typically around 0.6 to 1 beat per second in the middle octave, so that the 1.955-cent narrowing is applied consistently: the craft consists of laying one octave with prescribed beat speeds and then tuning outward in octaves. A few practical points follow. Tune upward into a note rather than downward onto it, since strings and pegs settle better under increasing tension. Always retune after a large change, because instruments with several strings share a body under tension and adjusting one alters the others. Allow an instrument to reach room temperature before tuning, because wind instruments in particular rise sharply in pitch as they warm, by roughly 3 cents per degree Celsius, which is why an orchestra retunes after the first movement and why a cold flute plays flat. Beating explains several effects that have nothing to do with error. Deliberate mistuning is a compositional resource: the characteristic shimmer of an accordion, a honky-tonk piano, a celeste rank or a chorus pedal is produced by two nearly identical sources beating at a few hertz, and the Javanese gamelan builds the same phenomenon into its paired instruments on purpose. The distinction between a slow beat that sounds rich and a fast one that sounds sour is roughly the boundary between fluctuation and roughness, somewhere near six to twenty beats per second depending on register. Understanding that boundary turns tuning into a controlled craft: you are not chasing an abstract correctness but placing a beat rate where you want it.

sections.heading: Where the Model Breaks: Inharmonicity, Bells and Gamelan
sections.body: The tidy picture of exact whole-number harmonics assumes an ideal string with no stiffness and an ideal air column with no complications, and real objects only approximate that. The most important departure in Western music is piano inharmonicity. A real steel string resists bending as well as stretching, and that stiffness raises the frequency of the higher modes above their ideal values according to the relation that the nth partial equals n times the fundamental times the square root of one plus B times n squared, where B is an inharmonicity coefficient depending on the string's diameter, length and material. B is small in a concert grand with long strings, perhaps 0.00005 in the middle, and much larger in a short spinet or in the thick, stubby bass strings any small piano is forced to use. The consequence is that a piano's second harmonic is measurably sharper than an exact octave, and tuners must therefore stretch the tuning to match: octaves are set slightly wider than 2:1 so that the fundamental of the upper note matches the sharp second partial of the lower. Accumulated over the keyboard this produces the Railsback curve, documented by O. L. Railsback in 1938, in which a well-tuned piano's top notes sit up to 30 or 40 cents sharp of equal temperament and its lowest notes similarly flat. A piano tuned to a mathematically perfect equal temperament sounds wrong. Percussion departs much further. An ideal circular drumhead has modes in the ratios 1, 1.59, 2.14, 2.30, 2.65 and so on, which are not whole numbers at all, so a drum has no definite pitch. Timpani are a partial exception: the kettle and the enclosed air load the membrane and shift several modes towards ratios near 1, 1.5, 2 and 2.44, close enough to a harmonic series that the ear assigns a clear pitch. Church bells are inharmonic by design, with named partials — hum, prime, tierce, quint and nominal — in approximate ratios of 0.5, 1, 1.2, 1.5 and 2. The tierce at 1.2 is a minor third, which is why traditional bells sound faintly mournful whatever the tune; major-third bells were only achieved in the 1980s using computer modelling of the bell profile. The Javanese and Balinese gamelan goes furthest. Its bronze metallophones and gongs have strongly inharmonic partials, and its scales, the five-note slendro and seven-note pelog, are not derived from small whole-number ratios and vary from one gamelan to the next, each set tuned as a unit with no universal reference pitch. Paired instruments are even detuned from each other by a few hertz on purpose, producing the shimmering beat called ombak. William Sethares argued in 1993 that a culture's preferred scale tends to match the spectrum of its instruments; the idea is influential and elegantly explains the gamelan case, though how far it accounts for musical practice generally remains debated.

sections.heading: Hearing It for Yourself, and Common Misconceptions
sections.body: Everything described here can be verified with objects most people already own, and doing so converts a set of assertions into direct experience. Before that, several persistent misunderstandings are worth clearing away. The first is the overtone numbering muddle: the second harmonic is the first overtone, because overtones count only the partials above the fundamental. Say harmonic and give the number, and the ambiguity disappears. The second is the belief that harmonics are added to a note by the instrument's body or by good technique. They are not; they are present from the instant the string or air column starts moving, because they are simply the shapes that fit, and what a soundboard does is radiate some more efficiently than others. The third is the idea that the seventh or eleventh harmonic is out of tune. They are exactly where physics puts them; it is the twelve-note keyboard that has no key for them. The fourth is the assumption that A equals 440 hertz is natural. It is an administrative decision of the twentieth century, and historical pitch ranged over more than a semitone; claims that 432 hertz has healing properties have no support in evidence. The fifth is the notion that consonance is pure convention. Sensory consonance has a measurable mechanism in harmonic coincidence and critical bandwidth, though musical consonance is genuinely cultural.
steps: Take a guitar or other stringed instrument. Touch a string very lightly directly over the twelfth fret, halfway along, pluck, and lift your finger. You will hear a clear bell-like tone an octave above the open string: the second harmonic.
Repeat over the seventh fret, a third of the way along, for the third harmonic, an octave and a fifth above; then the fifth fret, a quarter of the way, for the fourth harmonic, two octaves up.

Now pluck the open string beside the bridge, then over the fingerboard. The pitch is identical but the tone changes completely, from thin and bright to round and dark. You have altered which harmonics are excited, not which note is played.

At a piano, silently depress a chord of low keys so their dampers lift, hold them, and sing a loud short note. Listen after you stop: the strings whose harmonics match your note will be ringing back at you.
Blow across the top of an empty bottle, then add water and blow again. The pitch rises because the air column is shorter, and because a bottle is a closed pipe the change is larger than you expect.
Sound two strings or two tuners set to nearly the same frequency together. Count the beats per second: that number is the difference in hertz. Tune one slowly until the beating stops.
Hum steadily and slowly change your mouth from an ee to an oo while holding the pitch. The pitch stays; the timbre changes. You are moving formants across a fixed harmonic series.
With any spectrum or spectrogram app, play a flute-like tone, a clarinet and a square wave and compare the patterns of lines. The missing even harmonics of the last two are visible immediately.

guides.title: Tablature, Chord Charts and Lead Sheets
guides.summary: A comprehensive guide to the three great shorthand notations of popular and folk music: tablature, which shows where to put your fingers; chord charts and diagrams, which name and shape harmony; and lead sheets, which carry a whole song on one page as melody, chords and lyrics.

sections.heading: Three Shorthands and Why They Exist
sections.body:
Most music that people actually play from a page today is not written in full standard notation but in one of three practical shorthands: tablature, chord charts, and lead sheets. Each solves a different part of the problem of getting music out of one head and into another, and each deliberately leaves out information that its users can supply for themselves. Understanding what each captures, and just as importantly what each omits, is the key to reading, writing, and choosing between them.

Standard notation, the five-line staff with its noteheads and rhythms, is a complete and instrument-neutral record: it specifies every pitch and every duration precisely and can represent any music for any instrument. That completeness is also its cost. It takes years to read fluently, it says which pitch to sound but not, on a guitar or lute, which of several possible strings and frets to use, and it is far more than a folk singer or a rock guitarist usually needs. The three shorthands trade some of that completeness for speed, accessibility, and a better fit to how particular instruments and musicians work.

Tablature, or tab, is a fingering map. Instead of telling you which pitch to play and leaving you to find it, it tells you exactly where to put your fingers on a fretted instrument, which string and which fret, and lets the pitch take care of itself. It is ideal for guitar, bass, ukulele, and the historical lute family, where the same note can be produced in several places and the choice matters. Chord charts and chord diagrams work at the level of harmony: they name or picture the chords a song uses, trusting the player to supply a rhythm and voicing. They are the natural notation for accompaniment, where what matters is the chord sequence, not a fixed arrangement. A lead sheet combines a single written melody line in standard notation with chord symbols above it and lyrics below, compressing an entire song onto one page and leaving the arrangement to the performer.
